title: Anti-aging Therapies Trigger Efficacy and Safety Concerns
subtitle: China Newsweek June 15, 2026
paragraphs: Anxiety over aging in China has

boosted an anti-aging market bursting with expensive treatments, such as therapeutic or double filtration plasma exchange, ozone treatments, stem cell injections and the so-called life extending "miracle drug" rapamycin. However, while these drugs and procedures are intended to treat human illnesses, such as kidney disease, autoimmune deficiency and chronic hepatitis, they have yet to be approved for anti-aging and anti-cancer use. Meanwhile, despite new rules unveiled by Chinese regulators, these therapies with obscure names and unclear effects on healthy bodies are still being provided by clinics, especially private ones. Experts say that aging should not be treated as a disease, but rather an irreversible natural process. A healthy lifestyle, marked by a balanced diet, regular exercise, sufficient sleep, no smoking and moderate alcohol, is more effective than any anti-aging therapy.

title: AI will Play as Partner, Not Substitute, in Human Job Market
subtitle: China Economic Weekly June 15, 2026
paragraphs: Despite AI's challenges to the job market, experts in China assure that instead of being formidable competitors, AI agents are ideal work partners. With AI taking mundane and entry-level jobs, human employees can develop more sophisticated skills. Truck drivers can become convoy navigators to lead automatic driving vehicles and a graphic designer can complete an entire project alone. Creativity and lifelong learning have replaced spoon-fed knowledge and professional skills as the new essential qualities for job hunters. Some professions, like scientists, strategic consultants, doctors and nurses, are irreplaceable because of their innovative nature or skills in addressing complicated scenarios. But demand for robot trainers and computing scheduler is increasing. In response to the transformation, some economists highlight the role of education, especially in rural areas, calling it a springboard to boost potential innovations.

title: Low-Altitude Flight Risk Regulated as Sector Grows
subtitle: Fangyuan Magazine April 1, 2026
paragraphs: China has drafted and issued a number of laws, regulations and guidelines to regulate low-altitude flight, a complete new economic driver with rapid development. Incorporating electronic vertical take-off and landing vehicles (eVTOLs) and unmanned aircraft at altitudes below 3,000 meters, low-altitude flight has sparked immense safety concerns, such as intrusion of drones into restricted areas, disruption to passenger flights, damage to high-voltage power lines and scaring off wildlife in nature reserves. In many cases, there were no laws to govern unmanned flights nor certified training for operators. On January 1, the new Public Security Law included the low-altitude economy. Flight violators can face detentions of up to 10 days. Experts warn that since evidence of low-altitude aviation offenses is held in data in vehicles and drones, it requires quick and targeted responses from investigators.

title: Single-minded Youth Reshape: Dynamics of Big Cities
subtitle: Yi Magazine | June 5, 2026
paragraphs: Nowadays, China's young urban dwellers are not satisfied to just be major contributors to consumption and labor forces, who had been expected to provide as large a demographic dividend as previous generations of workers. Sticking to their own preferences, these young people are not so tempted by the delights of big metropolises. As trailblazers for industrial upgrades, frontier-tech users and new job creators, young people no longer compete for major resources exclusive to the biggest cities. Today, they can either work in megacities to enjoy all the facilities and entertainment they provide, or they can support themselves in simplicity and stability beyond them. To secure their sustainable development, cities, regardless of size, are starting to create inclusive, innovative and differentiated climates for young groups, which are declining in numbers. Experts suggest that cities pay particular attention to what attracts young people, such as flexible migration policies.

title: Young People Hesitant to Marry due to Unbearable Burdens
subtitle: People's Tribune | May 28, 2026
paragraphs: Declining birth rates in today's graying society are a reflection of young Chinese people's anxieties over getting married and having children. According to a 2025 survey by Peking University, despite young women's desire for romance, they are unlikely to enter into marriage without weighing the costs and potential risks, as women are traditionally seen to have larger roles in the family. Regardless of how independent Chinese women are, especially those between 20-24, they still factor in men's incomes, jobs and social networks before accepting a marriage proposal. Many young men, particularly those from less developed or rural areas, are hesitant to marry as well, because of the intolerable cost of bride gifts. Young people are more willing to solve their relationship problems by consulting AI. Experts suggest the country update policies to boost the confidence of young people to tie the knot.

title: VERBATIM
paragraphs: "China-EU relations today are defined by a coexistence of ice and fire. Rising tariff barriers and expanding protectionist legislation represent thickening ice, while sustained foreign direct investment in China, the urgent need for a green transition and a shared commitment to the multilateral system form an underlying warm current. Despite persistent structural challenges, the two sides remain deeply bound by common interests. The real question is not whether to cooperate, but in which areas and under what rules."

Liu Xiaochun, vice president of the Shanghai Finance Institute, at a forum on China's role amid global industrial restructuring hosted by CF40 on June 12.

Xue Lan, member of the State Council, dean of Tsinghua University's Institute for International Governance of Artificial Intelligence and China Institute for Science and Technology Policy, writing for the academic series Development and Governance of Digital Economy

No matter how satisfying the plot, how ruthless the protagonist's revenge or how spectacular their meteoric rise, audiences struggle to genuinely relate to their experiences."

title: New Circular Economy Blueprint to Aid Green Transition
paragraphs: China has published a new blueprint for the circular economy, aiming to develop a high-quality recycling system by 2030.

The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), the country's top economic planner, released the 15th Five-Year Plan for Circular Economy Development in July, which will guide resource recycling from 2026 to 2030.
The guideline envisions a full closed-loop industrial and social system to safeguard the supply security of national resources and advance a comprehensive
green
economic transition.

As defined by China's Circular Economy Promotion Law, a circular economy shifts from the traditional linear model of material use, manufacture and discard, to a sustainable loop centered on the "reduce, reuse and recycle" principles. Reduce means cutting raw material input and waste generation at the production stage, reuse means extending product service life via repair, remanufacturing and secondhand circulation, and recycle means recycling used products and converting solid waste and scrapped materials into reusable industrial raw materials. A circular economy features low consumption, low emissions, high efficiency and is environmentally friendly for more sustainable development.

The new circular economy plan has set clear targets to be fulfilled by 2030: Major resource productivity will rise about 16 percent compared to 2025, annual comprehensive utilization volume of bulk solid waste will reach 4.5 billion tons, annual recycled volume of core renewable resources will reach 510 million tons, and total output value of the resource recycling industry will expand to 8 trillion yuan (US$1.8t). By 2035, a high-quality circular economy system with globally leading resource utilization efficiency is expected to be fundamentally established.

To realize those targets, the plan proposes to promote green production and green consumption as well as green design and packaging, prioritize the efficient recycling and utilization of industrial resources, advance eco-circular development in agriculture and forestry, promote green construction throughout the whole engineering and construction process, boost the import and utilization of high-quality recycled raw materials from overseas, standardize the circulation and trading of secondhand goods and optimize targeted recycling capacity for key categories of waste.

Compared to previous documents, this plan for the first time proposes to foster and expand the circular economy services sector and incorporate waste generated from new infrastructure such as computing power facilities into the circular utilization system.
The plan stresses the need to improve end-of-life management and recycling networks for retired batteries, decommissioned wind power equipment, scrapped photovoltaic devices and other related waste.
Authorities will also revise China's Circular Economy Promotion Law to strengthen the legal force and release unified standards and evaluation indicators for local circular economy performance.

At a press conference on July 3 in Beijing, NDRC officials said that in 2025, China's national major resource productivity surged roughly 77 percent compared with 2012. The comprehensive utilization rate of bulk solid waste exceeded 60 percent, and the annual recycling volume of major renewable resources hit 410 million tons. Meanwhile, waste steel and nonferrous metals made up 27 percent and 30 percent of total industrial raw materials used in production, with the output value of the resource recycling industry hitting 5 trillion yuan (US$734.7b), a 10 percent annual growth.

NDRC officials emphasized that the plan is a priority as China is entering a core phase for high-quality development, green transition and realizing its carbon targets. China aims to peak carbon emissions by 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060.

title: Easier Tax Refunds Expected to Boost Tourism in Southern Regions
paragraphs: Five Chinese provincial regions, including Hunan, Fujian, Guangdong and Hainan provinces, as well as Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, have confirmed full mutual recognition of instant tax refunds.

Effective from July 1, the new policy allows foreign visitors and those from China's Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan regions to purchase and claim instant refunds at any designated shop or site in the five approved areas, and they can depart from anywhere within the five regions. It means visitors will no longer have to return to the original purchase site for departure.
The policy is intended to do away with previous regional restrictions and help tourists be more flexible with their itineraries. It is hoped it will promote consumption and expand inbound tourism.

Official data showed that in the first quarter of 2026, China's immigration authorities recorded 185 million entries and exits, with over 72 million coming from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan, a 10.3 percent growth year-on-year, and over 21 million from foreign countries, a 22.3 percent year-on-year growth.

title: New Action Plan to: Stabilize, Upgrade: Foreign Investment
paragraphs: A new action plan to attract foreign investment was released on June 22, which includes measures to stabilize and optimize foreign direct investment (FDI) while attracting new investors.

The document has five priorities, including expanding market access, facilitating foreign investment procedures, upgrading investment promotion, improving service for foreign investors and optimizing the administration of foreign investment. Key highlights include increasing opening-up in the education, healthcare, finance and biotechnology sectors, optimizing rules for cross-border data flow and tax incentives for foreign investors to reinvest profits, as well as incentives for acquiring domestic enterprises, attracting foreign investors to set up R&D centers in China and equally implementing national treatment for all foreign enterprises in government procurement.
The document is expected to scale up the "Invest in China" brand by pledging consistent, predictable opening-up policies and promoting mutually beneficial global cooperation.

title: China, EU Reach Consensus on New Orientation for Economic & Trade Relations
paragraphs: China and the EU have agreed on a new defining orientation for their economic and trade relations: stable and balanced key trading partners, He Yadong, spokesperson of China's Ministry of Commerce said at a press conference on July 2.

The consensus was reached during the first meeting of the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultation Mechanism held in Brussels on June 29 between China's Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security and Interinstitutional Relations and Transparency Maroš Šefčovič.
The mechanism was established for four workstreams, including trade and investment balancing, export controls, intellectual property rights and WTO reform.

The two sides agreed to establish a joint monitoring mechanism to exchange relevant data, monitor trade flows and support technical work to improve transparency, enhance mutual trust and manage trade frictions.

They agreed that increased market access measures and initiatives can contribute to the balancing of the trade relationship. They also took note of the positive results of the China- EU export control dialogue regarding rare earth elements and other critical materials.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press briefing on June 30 that China and the EU are partners, not rivals, and cooperation is win-win in nature.

title: New Energy Vehicle Tax: Subsidies to Be Adjusted
paragraphs: China's

Ministry of Finance, the State Taxation Administration and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology issued an official announcement on July 2, adjusting tax incentives for energy-efficient and new energy vehicles (NEVs).

Effective as of January 1, 2027, the 50 percent vehicle and vessel tax cut for eligible energy-saving cars will be terminated. Meanwhile, full tax exemption will no longer apply to battery-electric vehicles for commercial use, plug-in hybrid vehicles and fuel cell vehicles for commercial use. All such vehicles owned before or newly acquired after the policy shift should since then pay the taxes in full.
Given battery-electric passenger cars and fuel cell passenger cars do not have an engine whose volume relates to the tax, those vehicles remain outside the taxable scope.

Launched in 2012, tax incentives have greatly boosted NEV sales and industrial upgrading. Authorities noted the policy adjustment targets a fairer tax distribution amid mature development of NEVs, as sales in China accounted for more than 50 percent of total sales in 2025. Experts said that future preferential policies will likely target smallsized, light and energy-saving green vehicles.

title: Scientists Make ‘Artificial Sun' Breakthrough for Fusion Energy
paragraphs: Chinese scientists have announced a major breakthrough in ‘artificial sun' technology in the pursuit of creating energy through fusion.

The Institute of Plasma Physics at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science under the Chinese Academy of Sciences announced that two core superconducting magnets for fusion reactors have passed full acceptance and full working condition tests, with all core technologies 100 percent domestically developed.
The artificial sun is a man-made fusion facility that reproduces the sun's nuclear fusion reactions to develop clean, carbonfree and nearly inexhaustible fusion energy.

The toroidal field magnet, the globe's largest fusion reactor superconducting magnet weighing 582 tons, outperforms its ITER counterpart in southern France by 1.3 times in volume and three times in energy storage. It is used to prevent plasma from hitting the inner walls of the vacuum vessel.

Another critical component, the hightemperature superconducting central solenoid coil, also hit world-leading technical benchmarks. Acting like a spark plug and regulator for fusion plasma, it induces and drives the plasma current to ignite fusion reactions and heat fuel to super-high temperatures, while dynamically adjusting the plasma configuration to keep it stable.

Chinese scientists have been researching the components for six years, during which they have resolved global-level bottlenecks, including superconducting materials, precision manufacturing and radiation resistance, securing 47 patents and rolling out 14 industrial standards across the whole industrial chain.

title: Unofficial Child Sex Offender Registry: Draws Scrutiny For Exposing Victims' Info
paragraphs: A privately developed mini-app that functioned as an unofficial child sex offender registry sparked outcry in China for publishing the names and addresses of victims.

The WeChat mini-app, Child Sexual Harm Early Warning, referenced court records to show users the number of people convicted for sexual offenses against minors within a 50-kilometer radius of their location.

"There are 304 individuals with prior convictions for child sexual offenses living near you," Fan Yiyi, a young mother from Hebei Province, received in a screenshot shared in a parents' WeChat group, China Newsweek reported.

According to business inquiry platform Tianyancha, the mini-app is operated by Beijing Alliance Public Welfare Development Center, a registered non-profit that works with charity and social institutions.

The mini-app allowed users to access records that include offenders' full names, addresses, criminal charges and "risk level," as well as offering a 19.9 yuan (US$2.9) per month subscription tier with real-time alerts and more detailed profiles of convicted offenders.

According to reports, the Center voluntarily removed these functions following user complaints over the explicit case details they revealed, along with victims' full names and crime scene locations, which were sometimes their own homes.

Users also discovered that the number of convicted sex offenders shown referred only to their registered addresses or the locations of crimes listed in court verdicts, rather than their actual current locations.

That is partly because the data it published is outdated. Launched in 2015, the app cooperated with public security authorities for access to the data through a third-party platform. But that partnership has ended "for a long time," a public security spokesperson told newspaper Modern Express in May.
While China also has an official child sex offender database, public access is strictly limited.

Most netizens were united in criticizing the mini-app over the dangers of exposing victims' information, but opinions were divided over the disclosure of offenders' information. Some support making detailed information about child sex offenders public, while others argue that convicted criminals also have privacy rights. title: High Gaokao Scorer Loses Points with Public Over Interview Remark
paragraphs: Han Yaping of Central China's Henan Province went viral in June after scoring 699 out of 750 in the national college entrance examination (also known as the gaokao). Coming from a disadvantaged rural background, Han's exceptional score eventually landed her a spot at her first choice, Tsinghua University.

However, a remark she made during an interview took some shine off her success. When asked for any advice for fellow students on avoiding mobile phone addiction, Han said, "If you are unwilling to endure the hardships of studying, you will eventually have to endure the struggles of life."

Han has indeed faced hardships. Her mother has been bedridden for years with spinal arthritis, while her father supports the family through farming and odd jobs. Han did not own a mobile phone and could not afford to pay for exam prep courses.

But many viewed her comment as preachy. One comment on Sina Weibo read, "Congratulations on your good grades, but who are you to lecture me?" The comment received more than 500,000 likes and quickly fueled heated debate.
In the past, stories about high achievers like Han overcoming difficulties served as inspiring examples. But similar narratives and remarks are increasingly being perceived as condescending.

Media commentators said the reaction reflects changing perceptions of social fairness, which have weakened the long-held belief that hard work inevitably leads to success. When ordinary people realize they may struggle to replicate such rags-to-riches stories, their empathy may be replaced by frustration, cynicism and fatigue.

title: Cheng Lesong
paragraphs: Cheng Lesong's commencement speech at Peking University once again captured attention nationwide for keeping it real.
"Forgive me for not showering you with piles of flowery adjectives to offer my blessings," Cheng, chair of the school's philosophy department, told his graduating class on June 26.
Cheng's familiarity with internet memes and self-deprecating humor has earned him widespread appreciation for breaking away from the image of the aloof intellectual.

"We teachers, who are forced to take part in the annual graduation speech-writing competition, are trapped in deep anxiety and panic. We try hard to hide our secret relief at finally sending this huge annual hassle away, while putting on a show of reluctant nostalgia and delivering pompous, empty motivational clichés. None of this truly stresses us out, for we are seasoned old-timers with masterful acting skills," he said in his speech.

Born in 1978 in Dexing, Jiangxi Province, Cheng earned his PhD in cultural and religious studies at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. His research focuses on early Daoist thought, medieval Daoism and intellectual history during the Western and Eastern Han dynasties (202 BCE-220 CE).

This was not the first time Cheng's speeches won over the public. His commencement speech in June 2025 also went viral, particularly his reflections on philosophy as a way of life. In September 2025, his speech at the university's opening ceremony also attracted widespread attention.

Addressing freshmen, Cheng advised: "My suggestion for you is that even if you fail to focus on your studies, do not flit from one campus event or social gathering to another like a social butterfly. Having too many choices is essentially the same as having none at all."

Media commentators said Cheng's appeal lies in his ability to avoid complicated academic language and patronizing lectures. Rather than promoting unrealistic ambitions, he connects philosophical reflections with students' real-life concerns through a lighthearted and humorous style, encouraging them to live authentically and better understand themselves.

title: Norwegian Soccer Star Scores Big on Chinese Social Media
paragraphs: Amid his spectacular World Cup performance, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland has unexpectedly found social media fame in China. From short videos about cheat meals to hydration breaks, the contrast between his striking stature, formidable performance on the pitch and goofy off-field personality has won over legions of soccer fans.

Since joining Chinese social media in early June, Haaland has engaged with memes created by fans, who affectionately call him "Habao" (ha is the first syllable of his surname, and bao means "treasure." Together they mean a lovable goofball). Haaland has also shown followers how to style his signature man-bun and posted numerous humorous short videos.

Haaland also used Chinese rock singer Wu Bai's iconic song "Norwegian Wood" in his posts, immediately winning more points with locals. Free from the distant or arrogant image sometimes associated with global sports superstars, Haaland's down-to-earth interactions have endeared him with millions. He has more than 6.23 million followers on Douyin as of mid-July, more than Norway's total population of 5.6 million, while related topics on RedNote have generated nearly 1.8 billion views.

title: Prison Arts Programs: Creative Release
byline: By Wang Yan and Xie Xuewei
paragraphs: eleased
from
Shanghai's
Qingpu Prison in November 2020 after serving nearly 10 years, 34-year-old Wang Bin opened a jade carving studio using skills he learned in prison.

Convicted of home invasion robbery in 2012, he joined the prison's art rehabilitation program taught by veteran artisans, mostly volunteers from outside the jail, at the in-house Qingliu Jade Carving Studio.

He began sketching and soon immersed himself in art, drawing nightly in his cell to develop his own minimalist style. Training daily in the carving workshop, he mastered his craft, creating jade gourds, plants, birds and flowers, all the while regaining his confidence. His early work was flawed: the carving was uneven and initial replicas were only 40 to 50 percent accurate. He also made up to 30 draft ox sculptures for a single final piece.

With family funding, Wang invested over 3 million yuan (US$443,000) to launch his multi-service studio in late 2020. It offers jade carving, bamboo engraving, pigment painting and tea sales, and undertakes all the outdoor mural projects across Shanghai's Chongming Island.
Blank Slate

Thirty years ago, Shanghai prison authorities launched a pioneering art therapy rehabilitation program. The new RQingpu Prison mainly held long-term violent offenders who had issues with impulse control and anger management. They were prone to fights and assaults. To aid their rehabilitation and social reintegration, the prison introduced jade carving training.

Jade holds a unique sacred and cultural place in China's civilization. Originating from ancient rituals, it is far more than decoration, embodying traditional ethics, beliefs and aesthetics. Jade carving requires sustained focus and careful polishing, and traditional jade culture reshapes inmates' values. Jade culture promotes gentleness, tolerance and modesty, which helps people regain self-control and stability.

A Tongji University graduate in gemstone craft, prison officer Ni Lili joined the jade carving workshop to lead the art rehabilitation program. Having majored in jewelry production, Ni told NewsChina that inmates struggle through two tough stages: New arrivals feel lost about the future, while those nearing release live in severe anxiety. Art therapy can ease both transitions.

A valued intangible cultural heritage, jade carving shapes rough stone into exquisite art through meticulous craftsmanship. Transforming untrained inmates into skilled carvers once seemed unachievable. Initially struggling with the tools, they were gradually able to focus on the craft, guided by prison staff.

The program became more professional after officer Ni joined in March 2013. That year, inmate works won silver and excellence awards at Shanghai's Jade Dragon Award, a national jade carving contest hosted by the Shanghai Gem & Jade Industry Association. Over the next decade, the prison's Qingliu Jade Carving Workshop earned many honors. In 2024, two creations from the workshop titled Heart's Meditation and Good Tidings took gold and silver at the 16th edition of the awards, the first national gold prize earned by a Chinese prison art program.

While still incarcerated in 2018, Wang Bin's jade pendant Two Dragons Chasing a Pearl took bronze at the awards. Judges commended its balanced symmetry and fine openwork, as well as his skill at creating rich depth on ultra-thin jade slabs.

The Qingliu workshop stands out not only for jade carving training but also for its people-centered rehabilitation that combines empathy, guidance, discipline and counseling. According to Shanghai Prison Administration Bureau in August 2024, staff view inmates as flawed fine jade: Just as artisans assess raw jade, they explore each inmate's background and values to help them reshape themselves.
Most instructors are volunteers, supported by art-trained prison officers. All jade works are made to commercial order.

On a February morning, the reporter witnessed over 30 inmates begin work, grinding jade and refining sketches in the workshop. Guest master craftsmen reviewed and revised designs. Training follows a strict schedule: carving practice in the morning, error correction in the afternoon and sketching practice in cells each evening. Weekly assessments require all unsatisfactory pieces to be reworked.
Artistic Effect

Qingpu Prison offers diverse art rehabilitation and cultural courses. Since 2011, it has launched training in jade carving, bamboo engraving, embroidery, paper cutting, model making, calligraphy, shadow puppetry and oil painting, adopting a work-study-employment model to help inmates learn new skills during their sentences.

Art rehabilitation has spread across Shanghai's prisons. Tilanqiao Prison runs 14 programs including tai chi, folk music, cloisonné and various carving crafts. Baoshan Prison in Shanghai's Baoshan District introduced purple clay teapot making in 2015 and from 2023 to 2025, 14 inmates earned national ceramic firing technician certifications, boosting their employment prospects after release.

Nationwide, prisons in Hunan, Liaoning, Fujian and Henan provinces have also rolled out similar initiatives, offering instruction in performing comedy skits, Peking opera, paper cutting, calligraphy and painting.

Global research proves art therapy helps inmates regulate their moods, build social skills and problem-solving. Australian art therapy practitioner Sarah Tucker writes in Therapeutic Prison Art Interventions that prison art eases emotional distress, fosters self-awareness and resilience, rebuilds dignity and identity, and is effective in breaking the cycle of reoffending.

A Chinese researcher based in Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, who asked for anonymity, conducted a review of 25 international studies from 1995 to 2017, which found that art rehabilitation enhances vocational training, cuts in-prison misbehavior and reduces recidivism.

Qingpu Prison's three-decade jade carving program has achieved a zero reoffending rate among participants. Shanghai prison official Yang Guoqiang told NewsChina that there are clear gaps in recidivism rates between participants and non-participants, calling for wider adoption of effective art rehabilitation programs.
Ni Lili said that none of Qingpu's over 300 trained former inmates have reoffended. Over 80 percent work in jade carving and related fields, with several opening their own studios and shops.
Shaped Expertise

Many people mistakenly view art rehabilitation as hobby classes. According to criminologist Su Mingyue, art rehabilitation is a standardized management program governed by strict selection criteria, phased goals, rules and assessments.

Cai Xiaoling, director of education and rehabilitation at Shanghai Prison Administration Bureau, told NewsChina that participation in art programs never lowers prison management standards. All inmates abide by identical supervision, labor and daily conduct rules, and art activities are primarily arranged during their spare time.

Ni Lili serves as supervisor of Qingliu Jade Carving Workshop. He earned his degree in gem materials and technology from Tongji University in Shanghai in 2011 and passed the civil service exam the following year to become a prison officer. He used to worry his professional expertise would go to waste behind prison walls until he learned about Qingpu Prison's jade carving rehabilitation program.

Launched in 1994, this initiative was the first of its kind across China's prison system, and Ni's arrival greatly boosted its development. He learned from senior officers, veteran carvers and even skilled inmate artisans to refine his own jade carving techniques.

In its early days, the workshop only handled basic jade processing, and its works gained little market recognition. While honing his own craft, Ni taught inmates professional jade carving theory. He also invited university lecturers and master carvers to deliver on-site lectures. Under his guidance, inmates developed exquisite craftsmanship, creating works defined by fine details, elegant aesthetics and simple, pure styles.

"Jade carving demands total dedication, patience and perseverance to produce fine pieces," Ni Lili said in an August 2025 interview with the Legal Daily. "Inmates are at the lowest point of their lives, often with distorted views of right and wrong, honor and disgrace. Carving jade is ultimately about rebuilding one's inner self." He added that working with noble jade every day helps troubled inmates clear their minds and find a new life direction.

The workshop now has 34 trainees. Ni has helped them overcome technical challenges, secured its membership in the Shanghai Gem & Jade Trade Association, and partnered with leading industry firms to introduce advanced techniques and sustain stable production, raising the profile of the prison's jade artworks.

In 2025, Ni and one inmate were awarded the title of Shanghai-style Jade Carving Master by the Shanghai-style Jade Carving Culture Association. More than 20 inmates have obtained the same title. Their transformation is a remarkable achievement for China's prison art rehabilitation work.

A collaborative award-winning piece titled Mindful Thoughts, created by Ni and an inmate surnamed Li, is displayed at the workshop entrance. Yet Ni does not regard it as his finest work. "To me, the true masterpieces are the released inmates who have turned over a new leaf," he said.

Selecting suitable participants remains a major practical challenge for art rehabilitation programs. Cai Xiaoling said that such initiatives pursue two core objectives: stabilizing the mental state of longterm inmates and equipping them with employable skills. Painting and carving help build focus and self-discipline, while mural painting, which is easier to learn and has more demand, can help released inmates find jobs more easily.

Besides voluntary applications, prison staff screen inmates based on their background, daily performance, sentence and offense type. Young, outgoing inmates can join performance teams, while violent and long-term offenders take up carving training. A peer mentorship system sees experienced participants guide new arrivals. Those lacking talent or interest may opt out.

Overall, art rehabilitation represents an advanced approach to inmate correction. While upholding strict prison safety rules, it gives inmates a chance to restart their lives. As criminologist Su Mingyue points out, officers leading art programs are first and foremost prison personnel proficient in law enforcement and supervision. Art is simply a tool to facilitate inmate education and rehabilitation.

For Su, the more pressing challenge is the shortage of qualified professionals. Only a small number of prison officers have formal art education backgrounds, so most prisons rely heavily on external professionals to run these programs, most of them volunteers.

An official from the education and rehabilitation division of Hunan Provincial Prison Administration told NewsChina that outside instructors usually work on a temporary basis, making long-term program continuity hard to guarantee. In contrast, full-time prison officers with art expertise engage in daily management and rehabilitation work year-round. They are better positioned to observe inmates' behavior, monitor their mental conditions and deliver targeted guidance.

Another fundamental problem is social stigma. Prison staff say social organizations are generally reluctant to participate, forcing prisons to take the initiative to seek external support. This hesitation stems from risk concerns as well as deepseated public prejudice against offenders. Low social acceptance, and even superstitious resistance to products made by inmates, create further barriers for exoffenders seeking employment.

To expand vocational training, Qingpu Prison has extended its programs beyond craft workshops to include an art troupe, media studio, high-end garment workshop and modern agricultural entrepreneurship park, while actively engaging social partners.
In January 2021, the prison signed cooperation agreements with five organizations across different fields, marking deeper integration with the community.

Li Qiang, Party secretary and warden of Qingpu Prison, said the work-studyemployment rehabilitation model serves social stability by linking inmate reformation, social reintegration and post-release employment.

Production work encourages inmates to earn an honest living through labor. Systematic study and training motivates active learning and broadens their horizons. For employment support, the prison helps released inmates assess their strengths and weaknesses, access job and entrepreneurship guidance and develop rational career plans.
Carving Out

In April, the 22nd meeting of the 14th National People's Congress Standing Committee conducted the third review of the revised Prison Law draft. Key revisions focus on strengthening inmate education and rehabilitation, and advancing the cause toward greater professionalism and social participation. Against this backdrop, prisons nationwide have rolled out recruitment drives targeting arts majors this year, attracting broader public attention. Hunan Province's prison system has advertised 18 positions for arts graduates, while Shandong, Anhui, Guangdong, Gansu and other provinces have launched similar recruitment initiatives. The recruits will primarily still work as prison officers.

Anhui Women's Prison noted in its 2026 recruitment notice that frontline roles cover prison cultural development, inmate education, rehabilitation and logistical support. Jinan Jiteng Prison in Shandong further specified required majors including musicology, music and dance performance in its 2025 recruitment plan.

Hunan took the lead in hiring arts professionals for correctional work as early as 2004. While law and medicine remain core recruitment majors, artsrelated positions are flexibly allocated by individual prisons based on operational needs, primarily to deliver art rehabilitation programs. Prison officer Hu Yan, who works in the Hunan prison system, told NewsChina that newly recruited arts graduates must complete around two years of training in police work, law and correctional management before applying their professional skills on the job.

Prison officers and criminology scholars told NewsChina that modern prison governance adheres to the principle of combining punishment with rehabilitation. Art activities guide inmates to engage in self-reflection and correct their conduct, ultimately helping them rejoin society as law-abiding citizens.
In a July 2021 interview with The Paper, Wang Bin said he wanted to pass on his carving skills.

He employs rehabilitated ex-offenders and people with disabilities, requiring all staff to stay away from gambling and other vices. Li Fei, a former inmate who now lives in Shanghai, assists with studio management, volunteer work and resource coordination. He has taken on a 28-year-old ex-inmate as an apprentice. Wang expects consistent mentorship over three to five years to attract more budding craftsmen.
"The past is beyond remedy, but we can still strive for a better future," Wang Bin told The Paper.
Wang Bin and Li Fei are pseudonyms

title: Go Global: Code Switch
byline: By Li Mingzi and Xu Ming
paragraphs: rom hospitals to supermarkets, Chinese-made robots are rapidly expanding their presence overseas.

In mid-June, Shanghai-based Fourier Intelligence deployed its robots at a physical therapy center run by Malaysia's Social Security Organization (Perkeso), where they support rehabilitation alongside human therapists for people recovering from workplace injuries and accidents.
The multi-million-yuan project marks a milestone for Chinese robotics companies in the global healthcare market.
A
month
earlier,

1.3-meter-tall FUnitree robots were photographed loading luggage onto conveyor belts at Haneda International Airport in Tokyo, Japan. They have been assisting with tasks since May, including aircraft towing and cargo loading, alongside Shenzhen-based UBTech's Walker E robot.

The industry has come a long way since China exported its first complete robot in 2007. Annual robot sales totaled just 9,738 units in 2014. In 2025, China's humanoid robot shipments had reached about 14,400 units, accounting for 84.7 percent of the global total, according to a report by the China Center for Information Industry Development and China Electronics News.

Exports of both humanoid and industrial robots entered a period of rapid growth in 2025, with industrial robot exports rising 48.7 percent year-on-year. In Q1 2026, exports of robots designed to clean floors, windows and pools reached 7.75 billion yuan (US$1.1b), or 68.5 percent of China's total robot export value, with shipments reaching 148 countries and regions.
Behind the export boom is a shift in strategy, especially among smaller firms.

"Rather than relying on low prices, Chinese companies are creating value overseas through integrated products and services, supported by a complete industrial supply chain," Li Zhiwei, who heads the international market division at Yunji Technology, a delivery robot manufacturer based in Beijing, told NewsChina.

But to gain staying power in these markets, companies still face challenges like regulatory compliance, customer trust and long-term product reliability. "Technology is only the admission ticket," Li added.
‘No Longer Optional'
Wang Kecheng, founder of construction robotics company Patner, landed his first overseas order in France after exhibiting at a trade show in 2024.
Their tile-laying robot was featured by local media, which caught the attention of a major construction company dealing with persistent labor shortages.
Patner only makes a tile-laying robot and a system that lays out survey lines to map out construction sites. Wang says this is a deliberate choice.
"They're both difficult products to develop, but they solve high-value problems in specific construction scenarios," Wang said. These conditions include covering large areas with simple perimeters.

The company claims their tile-laying robot works five to six times faster than a human worker while reducing overall construction costs by about 60 percent. By the end of 2025, Patner had received more than 10 million yuan (US$1.5m) in orders, with overseas markets accounting for 55 percent.

Labor shortages continue to drive demand, Wang said. In parts of Europe and the US, where building codes are strict, skilled tradespeople command high wages. Tile installers in the US average around US$25 an hour, and for custom work demand US$75 or more.

Landscaping is another growth area, and Shenzhen-based robotics company Mammotion is looking to cut in. The firm entered the robotic lawn mower market in 2022, competing against long-established European names like Husqvarna in Sweden and Germany's Bosch.

Most conventional robotic mowers require burying perimeter wires around property lines, making installation labor-intensive. Mammotion eliminated that step by adapting high-precision positioning technology originally developed for drones.

The innovation propelled the company to become the world's best-selling wire-free robotic lawn mower brand between July 2024 and June 2025, according to Frost & Sullivan. Its products are now sold in more than 30 countries and regions, serving over 400,000 homes.
Its wire-free mowers retail for US$2,599-4,999, roughly 50 percent more than conventional models.

"The higher price gives us room to keep investing in new technologies," said a Mammotion employee who works in developing international markets. Instead of competing through price cuts, the company is positioning itself as a premium brand before expanding market share. He described the company's strategy as "taking technology around the world to find scenarios where customers are willing to pay."

This approach appears to be reshaping the market. China's lawn mower exports reached 13.2 billion yuan (US$1.9b) in the first seven months of 2025, up 56.6 percent year-on-year, with wire-free models driving much of the growth.

"Global customers are under increasing pressure to reduce costs and improve efficiency," Xie Kaixuan, marketing director at Dobot Robotics, told China Business Journal in May. "Chinese manufacturers benefit from deeply integrated supply chains that allow us to move quickly from order to delivery."

The Shenzhen-based company has established branches and R&D centers in more than 12 countries and regions. Its robots are used in over 200 applications across 15 industries, from auto manufacturing to medical surgery and retail.

"For many emerging robotics companies, going global is no longer optional," said Fan Yazhou, head of marketing at Wuhan-based Creatulize, which makes robotic mattress-cleaning systems. He noted that the company's founding team consists almost entirely of engineers born in the 1990s and 2000s, several having studied or worked overseas.
An industry insider with 12 years of international business experience told NewsChina that geopolitical tensions have changed how robotics startups expand.

"A decade ago, companies like [drone maker] DJI could focus on building great products before expanding overseas," he said. "Today's startups have to think about tariffs, export controls and data compliance from day one. If you wait until you've succeeded at home, the window may already have closed."
China's manufacturing base has made that possible.

Zhou Jian, founder and CEO of UBTech, previously told NewsChina that when the company was established 18 years ago, it relied on imported servo drives for consumer robots. Today, nearly every precision component can be sourced domestically from suppliers in the Pearl and Yangtze river deltas.

"Young entrepreneurs no longer have to build supply chains from scratch," Zhou said. "Even small production runs are affordable. They're building on top of an industrial ecosystem that already exists."
Brand Conscious
In recent years, crowdfunding has become an important launchpad for China's emerging robotics companies, providing an early testing ground for global demand and a way to build brand recognition.
In May 2022, Mammotion raised US$3.37 million on Kickstarter for its first wire-free robotic lawn mower, Luba.

"It wasn't just about raising money," said the Mammotion employee. Feedback from their backers helped refine the product, pushing the engineering team before mass production. "Those customers proved we'd solved a real problem," he said.

According to Kickstarter, the platform handled US$9.3 billion in pledges as of November 2025. Chinese creators accounted for 8.4 billion yuan (US$1.2b) of that total, making it the largest group outside the US.

"Chinese companies aren't just becoming better storytellers. They're becoming better brand builders," Henri Peng, Kickstarter China's chief strategy representative, told cross-border e-commerce platform Yuguo in late 2025.

After fulfilling its Kickstarter orders, Mammotion shifted its marketing strategy. Instead of focusing on engineering details, its advertising highlighted convenience, time savings and everyday use. They also worked with lifestyle influencers, who posted about using their products in homes and gardens.
"If any part of the process fails, delivery, storytelling or after-sales service, you'll lose far more than you raised through
crowdfunding,"
said
Fan Yazhou with Creatulize.

He said that while crowdfunding allows startups to enter overseas markets without immediately investing in warehouses or distribution networks, long-term success ultimately depends on building reliable service capabilities.
Going Local
Winning a contract overseas rarely happens overnight.
Fourier
Intelligence's
partnership with Malaysia began in 2022. According to founder and CEO Gu Jie, the relationship evolved gradually, starting with supplying individual products and R&D.

Localization was key to their strategy. Speaking to financial outlet Yicai, Gu said they added landmarks such as the Petronas Twin Towers and local street scenes in their robot-assisted physical therapy simulators for patients preparing to return to work and everyday life.
"Our advantages lie in our complete industrial chain, extensive real-world deployment experience and willingness to invest deeply in local markets," Gu said.

Several interviewees said that in developed markets, companies typically need two to three years before seeing meaningful returns. That commitment is even more crucial for younger companies still establishing their reputations.
Rather than relying on distributors, Mammotion established subsidiaries in the US and Germany, allowing it to respond more quickly to customer needs and provide localized after-sales services.
Shenzhen-based iKitbot has taken a similar approach in Japan.
Since entering the market in 2024, the commercial cleaning robot manufacturer has spent two years adapting its products to meet Japanese building standards.

Li Jianuo, president of iKitbot Japan, said Japan presents greater challenges than other major markets. "Japanese business culture is highly risk averse," she said. "Building trust takes time. But once you've earned it, you're very difficult to replace."
She added that success in Japan also strengthens credibility elsewhere.
Recognizing severe labor shortages and an underserved market for midsized
commercial
cleaning
robots, iKitbot conducted a two-month proofof-concept trial at major commercial properties before formally entering the market.
The trial revealed numerous design challenges.
Japan's

flame-retardant flooring absorbs water while remaining highly sensitive to heavy equipment, requiring substantially lighter robots. Highly reflective black floor tiles in high-end office buildings interfered with navigation systems, while dense floor markings complicated machine vision.

Meeting consumer expectations was equally demanding. To compete in the Japanese market, robots had to recover at least 95 percent of the water used to reduce slipping accidents, while making no more noise than an ordinary vacuum cleaner.

This required redesigning everything from hardware to algorithms, efforts that paid off. The company has since secured orders worth hundreds of millions of yen, expanding from luxury hotels into hospitals, retail chains and exhibition centers.

Today, about 90 percent of iKitbot's revenue comes from overseas markets, with Japan accounting for nearly half. The company is now applying the standards it developed there to expand into German-speaking countries and northern Europe.
"Trust isn't built with PowerPoint presentations," Li said. "It's earned by solving the hardest real-world problems."
Beyond Hardware
In a hospital in Bangkok, Yunji Technology's delivery robots navigate busy corridors, delivering medicines and laboratory samples with precision.

The company began by supplying delivery robots to hotels but is now expanding into more complex environments. "What customers care about is reliability and return on investment," Li Zhiwei said. "They don't care what the robots look like."

As competition intensifies, Yunji is moving toward AI-powered management systems. Revenue from its AI platform rose 57.3 percent year-on-year in 2025, accounting for nearly 30 percent of the company's total revenue.
This reflects a broader shift, as companies increasingly set up overseas subsidiaries and R&D centers to provide end-to-end solutions.

Dobot Robotics in Shenzhen, for example, offers customers services from site planning and systems integration to employee training and after-sales support. "The value is no longer just the robot itself," Xie Kaixuan of Dobot told China Business Journal in May.
As more Chinese companies expand overseas, competition is also ramping up. The interviewed Mammotion employee said customer acquisition costs have doubled since 2022.
"We're still growing the market together," he said. "But the next stage of competition will be defined by differentiated services, stronger brands and technological
innovation."
Features once considered premium, such as fourwheel drive in robotic lawn mowers, have already become standard, he said.
‘No Shortcuts'
Despite rapid growth, companies expanding overseas face increasingly complex regulatory hurdles. One of the biggest is data compliance.
As robots become more connected and software-driven, protecting customer data and complying with local privacy regulations have become as important as hardware, Li said.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation, for example, strictly limits transferring personal data outside the bloc unless specific legal safeguards are in place.
As many companies can no longer rely on China-based cloud platforms, they must build computing and datastorage infrastructure locally, further increasing overhead.
That has forced companies to prioritize privacy and security and tailor compliance for different markets.
At Yunji, for example, they partner with local operators in countries with strong data privacy laws, such as Japan and the US, who manage systems that prevent cross-border data transfers altogether.

Xie said operating, maintenance and after-sales service standards vary widely from country to country. In some markets, Chinese brands also continue to face stigma for producing low-end, cheap goods that can only be overcome through consistent product quality and reliable service.
"There are no shortcuts," Xie said. "We earn trust through every delivery, every day of reliable operation and every day of quality service."

title: Go Global: Expansion Drive
byline: By Chen Weishan and Yu Xiaodong
paragraphs: n June 2, BYD's vessel Zhengzhou arrived at Melbourne Port, completing its maiden voyage to Australia. Operated directly by the Chinese automaker, the ship delivered 4,809 BYD new-energy vehicles (NEV), setting a new record for the largest single shipment of NEVs imported into the Australian market.
Departing from Shanghai, the vessel covered approximately 9,756 kilometers over 14 days. It is one of eight Ocustomized
roll-on-roll-off
(RoRo) ships in BYD's expanding maritime fleet. The shipment also marked the company's first use of its own carrier to deliver vehicles directly to Australia.
Local BYD dealer Wang Hua in Melbourne said customers had been closely tracking the shipment, with delivery wait times for BYD vehicles in Australia typically stretching from six to eight weeks.

BYD's footprint in Australia has expanded rapidly over the past two years. In the first six month of 2026, the Chinese automaker became the country's second-best-selling car brand, behind Toyota. It is targeting 30,000 deliveries in the third quarter and nearly 100,000 units in annual sales this year, almost double its 2025 total.

BYD's overseas expansion reflects a wider rise of Chinese automakers, particularly in the NEV sector. Data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM) shows that in the first six months of 2026, China's automobile exports rose to 5.07 million units, up 65.3 percent year-on-year, while NEV exports, including electric and plug-in hybrid models, totaled 2.36 million units, up 120 percent from a year earlier, accounting for 46.2 percent of all auto exports.

Chery led Chinese automakers in exports in the first half of the year, with 943,800 vehicles shipped overseas, up 71.5 percent year-on-year. It was followed by BYD and SAIC Group, which posted overseas sales of roughly 789,400 and 734,700 units respectively, including both exports and locally produced vehicles, representing annual growth of 70.5 percent and 48.7 percent. Neither company breaks out export-only figures separately. Geely Auto, meanwhile, exported 474,200 vehicles over the period, up 158 percent year-on-year, the fastest growth among major Chinese brands.

More importantly, Chinese auto brands are not only shipping more vehicles overseas, but building a more visible presence, including operating directly controlled dealerships and aftersale services and establishing factories.

As Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the China Passenger Car Market Information Association, noted in an article he posted on his WeChat account in February, China's auto industry has been shifting from products going overseas to supply chains going overseas.
New Energy
A key driver behind the surge of Chinese NEV exports has been soaring fuel prices amid heightened tensions in the Middle East.

In Australia, as gasoline prices rose by roughly 40 percent in March, batteryelectric vehicles' share in the new car market increased to 14.6 percent, with Chinese-made vehicles, including Tesla models produced in Shanghai, capturing roughly 80 percent of NEV sales. In the month, BYD entered Australia's top three brands for the first time, recording monthly sales of 7,217 vehicles and growth of around 50 percent.

According to Wang, NEV owners in Australia can reduce operating costs by 30 to 40 percent compared with traditional gasoline vehicles. "The energy crisis has acted as a catalyst," he said. "Previously, families often hesitated between gasoline and electric vehicles. Now more consumers are actively choosing NEVs to escape rising fuel costs."

The Australian market is following a global surge in electric vehicle adoption. According to S&P Global Mobility, 28 of 150 countries with available data, including Australia and the UK, posted record monthly electric vehicle (EV) sales in March, while nine nations, among them Brazil and the Philippines, set new highs in April. Over the two-month period, EV sales surpassed year-earlier levels in 91 percent of all markets tracked. This was the first time since April 2023 that more than 90 percent of countries recorded year-on-year growth.

In Europe, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association showed that registrations of batteryelectric vehicles, plug-in hybrid-electric vehicles and hybrid-electric vehicles across the 31 markets comprising the EU, the European Free Trade Association and the UK rose by 39.1 percent, 13.2 percent and 8.2 percent year-onyear, respectively, in May.

In a Bloomberg opinion piece published on May 26, columnist David Fickling argued that just like the 1970s oil crisis reshaped the global auto industry by undermining large, fuel-inefficient vehicles and accelerating the rise of smaller, more fuel-efficient Japanese cars, today's geopolitical tensions in the Middle East could have a similar effect on electric vehicles, potentially sustaining their adoption even after conditions stabilize, as more consumers switch to EVs and experience their benefits firsthand.

Given China's leading position in the EV sector, many believe that the current energy crisis could push Chinese EVs to replicate Japan's success, transforming a temporary demand shock into a lasting structural shift.

The transformation is already underway, with Chinese EV makers in a position to capture the market. In Australia, Chinese automakers overtook Japan in February to become the largest source of newly sold vehicles, bringing an end to nearly three decades of Japanese dominance.

In Singapore, the shift has been even more striking. BYD surpassed Toyota as the country's best-selling car brand in 2025 and widened its lead in 2026. Data from Singapore's Land Transport Authority showed that BYD accounted for 26 percent of all new car registrations during the first five months of 2026, more than the combined 21.2 percent share of Toyota, Honda, Mazda and Nissan.

Also in May, Chinese passenger car brands overtook their Japanese counterparts across the 31 European countries in monthly new registrations for the first time, capturing a 12.01 percent market share, compared with 11.32 percent for Japanese brands.
Besides
mature

economies, Chinese automakers are actively exploring emerging markets. In the past few years, Uzbekistan has become a new battleground for Chinese carmakers. With a population of more than 36 million, the country is the largest and fastest-growing automobile market in Central Asia. Demand has more than doubled since 2021, with new vehicle sales exceeding 461,000 units in 2025.

For decades, the country's auto market was centered around one manufacturer, Chevrolet, which has a near monopoly with market share of over 90 percent through its local joint venture UzAuto Motors. But as Chinese automakers are entering the market, Chevrolet's dominance is declining.

In 2025, Chevrolet's market share dropped to 83.2 percent from 87.9 percent in 2024, while BYD, Chery and Haval, the top Chinese brands in the country, secured a market share of 10.3 percent. In the first quarter of 2026, Chevrolet's market share declined to 79.3 percent, while BYD's share surged to 8.6 percent.
Tougher Road

However, unlike Japanese automakers in the 1970s and 1980s, and South Korean manufacturers in the decades that followed, which expanded abroad during an era of accelerating globalization and relatively open markets, Chinese carmakers are entering a global arena marked by higher tariffs, trade investigations, supply chain realignments and intensifying geopolitical tension.

Chinese carmakers' success in Australia is an exception rather than the rule among developed Western markets, due to the free trade agreement between the two countries. The US, the world's second-largest automobile market, has imposed a 100 percent tariff on Chinese EVs, effectively closing its market to Chinese brands.

In the EU, the world's third-largest auto market, China-made EVs are subject to anti-subsidy duties of up to 35.3 percent, in addition to the bloc's standard 10 percent import tariff. While Chinese carmakers have continued to gain ground in the EU, raising their market share to about 10.5 percent in May, further expansion, particularly through exports, could become increasingly difficult amid persistent trade tensions between Beijing and Brussels. It is recently reported that the European Commission is considering extending its anti-subsidy duties to Chinese-made plug-in hybrids.

Chinese automakers also face a steep learning curve in building overseas sales networks, after-sales service systems and localized operations. With relatively small domestic markets, Japanese and South Korean automakers had to internationalize early and build their business models around exports and overseas production. Chinese carmakers, by contrast, matured in the world's largest automotive market and are only now making the transition from domestic champions to global competitors.

Without established overseas sales and service networks, many Chinese automakers initially relied on local distributors to market and sell their vehicles. While this strategy enabled rapid market entry, it often came at the expense of long-term brand building. Focused primarily on boosting sales, some distributors failed to provide adequate after-sales service and technical support, leaving customer complaints unresolved and, in some cases, damaging the reputation of Chinese brands.

Li Wei, who manages Jetour's first company-owned dealership in Uzbekistan, said the brand learned this lesson firsthand. Jetour, an independent marque under Chery, initially relied on local distributors, but many customers struggled to access reliable maintenance and repair services. The experience prompted the company to establish its own dealership network in the country to strengthen after-sales support and rebuild consumer confidence.

Pei Ruijie, Nio's national distributor in Uzbekistan, has been importing and selling Chinese vehicles in the country since 2022. He argues that exporting cars alone is not enough to build a lasting presence overseas.
"Automobiles are durable goods. Building a successful brand requires an entire ecosystem, including aftersales
service,
marketing,
technical support and local operations," he told NewsChina. "Simply selling cars does little to establish a brand."

The experience has underscored a broader shift taking place across China's auto industry. Having gained a foothold overseas through exports and local distributors, leading Chinese carmakers are now moving into a new phase by building their own distribution networks, service infrastructure and localized operations.

When BYD entered the Australian market in 2022, it relied on local automotive retailer Eagers Automotive as its exclusive importer, distributor and retail partner. Three years later, BYD revoked Eagers' exclusive rights, ended the distributorship of its former local partner, EVDirect, and took direct control of its sales and distribution in Australia
Localization Imperative

After learning how to sell cars overseas, Chinese automakers are now learning how to build businesses overseas. The trajectory mirrors that of Japanese and South Korean automakers, which also evolved from exporting vehicles through local distributors to establishing their own sales networks, manufacturing plants and supplier bases as they became global brands.

According to an executive at a Chinese automaker, the industry's globalization strategy typically unfolds in three stages. It begins with vehicle exports, followed by the establishment of overseas sales and marketing subsidiaries. Today, the industry has entered a third phase of deeper localization, with automakers investing in manufacturing, supply chains and other core operations while taking greater control of their overseas businesses.

BYD has emerged as one of the clearest examples of this strategy. In July 2024, the company opened its first wholly owned overseas passenger vehicle plant in Rayong, Thailand, a 150,000-unit facility serving as its manufacturing hub for Southeast Asia.

It has also established a joint venture in Uzbekistan to produce NEVs for the Central Asian market. In Latin America, BYD is investing about US$550 million to transform a former Ford plant in Camaçari, Brazil into a production base capable of producing 150,000 vehicles annually.

Europe, however, presents a different challenge. Faced with rising tariffs and higher production costs, Chinese automakers are pursuing a combination of greenfield investments and partnerships with established manufacturers. BYD is building its first European passenger vehicle plant in Szeged, Hungary, and has announced a second factory in Manisa, Turkey, both designed to supply the European market.

Building new factories is only one route to localization. Yang Yanding, general manager of strategic planning at Dongfeng Motor, argues that Europe's underutilized manufacturing base offers Chinese automakers an opportunity to expand more efficiently.

"Many overseas automakers are grappling with excess capacity, with some factories operating at only around 50 percent utilization. That gives Chinese companies an opportunity to make more efficient use of existing manufacturing resources," Yang told reporters at this year's Beijing Auto Show.
Rather than constructing new plants, he said, automakers can localize production through joint ventures, productioncapacity leasing or equity partnerships, depending on their business strategies.

That model is already taking shape. On May 20, Stellantis and Dongfeng signed a preliminary deal to establish a Europe-based joint venture covering sales, distribution, manufacturing, purchasing and engineering. The venture, which will be 51 percent owned by Stellantis, is expected to produce Dongfeng's Voyah-branded electric vehicles at Stellantis' underutilized plant in Rennes, France.

The agreement follows Stellantis' expanding partnership with China's Leapmotor. Initially focused on distribution, the two companies announced in May that they would extend their collaboration to manufacturing, with plans to produce Leapmotor vehicles at Stellantis' plant in Spain.

Together with the Dongfeng venture, the partnership signals a new phase in the globalization of China's auto industry. Rather than simply exporting vehicles, Chinese automakers are increasingly embedding themselves in overseas industrial ecosystems through local
manufacturing
and
strategic partnerships.

For Chinese automakers, building factories overseas is only the beginning. Their long-term success will depend on how well they integrate into local economies by creating jobs, developing supplier networks and adapting to local regulations and market conditions. Ultimately, the transition from exporting cars to building global businesses will determine whether they can establish themselves as lasting players in the global auto industry.

title: Go Global: Worth the Hype
byline: By Meng Qian and Xu Ming
paragraphs: In late April, Shenzhen municipal government announced that Wavytalk, a local beauty appliance brand, had earned over US$200 million in revenue from its US TikTok Shop in the past three years.

The company debuted with a sixsecond video featuring a girl using Wavytalk's curling iron on TikTok Shop. The video went viral, and around a thousand curling irons sold in just a day. "We never expected that video would bring such explosive sales. It had never happened before in all our years of crossborder business," Wavytalk founder Zou Xiu told NewsChina.
The company had been an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) for foreign companies for about a decade, before deciding to develop their own range.
With a strong supply chain at home, they built an edge based on their comprehensive product line and competitive prices. But rising tariffs, logistics and compliance costs are making it harder.

Like Wavytalk, many Chinese smalland medium-sized enterprises were invisible, acting as manufacturers for Western brands and retailers. Social media platforms have allowed them to compete on an equal footing, using sites like TikTok Shop, Facebook and Instagram. Employing content creators to assist them, they make emotional connections with consumers, allowing them to sell not just products, but lifestyle brands in overseas markets.
Proven Logic

Tianyuan Pet, a company based in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, made a 12-second video that went viral with over 10 million views. It shows a cat frantically scratching a sofa, the owner sighing in despair to a sad soundtrack. Suddenly, a cat tree slides into frame. The cat is instantly drawn to it, climbs up and curls up to sleep.

The clip does not introduce the actual cat tree, but still the comment section blew up, with people asking where to buy it and how much it was. The surge in orders demonstrated the power of emotional storytelling over traditional product pitches.

Cai Fengquan, who manages crossborder trade for Tianyuan Pet, said the company has been in business for many years. Some of their products bring in millions of US dollars a year on Amazon. But their brand barely had any name recognition.

That is a big problem for the scores of manufacturers scattered across industrial clusters in areas like the Pearl and Yangtze river deltas in eastern and southern China. They have long been trapped at the bottom of the global value chain, earning scant profits amid cutthroat competition. Despite their mature manufacturing and supply chain efficiency, they have little brand premium or pricing power.

Traditional e-commerce platforms cannot help them much. "What we found as the biggest ceiling to growth is that even though you can sell products, you can barely build brand awareness or earn customer loyalty," Wavytalk's Zou said in an interview with 36Kr, a tech and business news outlet.

On platforms like Amazon, consumers search for a specific item and a sea of similar-looking listings appears. They compare prices and reviews, and make purchase decisions. This exposes a fundamental flaw in the traditional model: Products are competitive only in price, making it hard for a new brand to stand out and build long-term assets.

On social media platforms, content and emotions come first. Users are not searching - they are scrolling for entertainment. In this environment, a 12-second cat video has an edge. This "content-first" approach allows brands to build an identity and a personal connection with consumers before a purchase is even considered.
In this new ecosystem, "content is the shelf and creators are the salespeople," Zou said.
As Cai Fengquan of Tianyuan Pet puts it, "Amazon solves the problem of selling goods, but TikTok solves the problem of being remembered."

"The biggest challenge for brands going global is getting consumers to recognize your name in the first place," Cai said. "In the past, that meant throwing money at Google Ads and Facebook, or hiring expensive overseas PR agencies to place articles. The costs were extremely high and results were hard to measure.
But today, a viral short video might cost little more than the time it takes to shoot and edit, and it can generate more reach than a million-dollar ad campaign.
Cai said that once a supply chain is in place, the missing piece is an arena where consumers can truly connect with and remember a brand.

Direct connection with consumers through video platforms allows manufacturers to get instant feedback and make timely adaptations to the market, particularly the overseas markets, where Chinese firms struggle to understand needs of consumers there.
Comments and interaction from consumers on platforms like TikTok Shop fill the gap. Wavytalk's bestselling curling iron was a direct result of this feedback.

"We determined there was strong consumer demand for this product, so we moved quickly to develop it as a separate product," Zou told 36kr. Previously, it had been sold as part of a set. Drawing on feedback from the comments, they added adjustable temperature settings and integrated negative-ion technology to combat frizz.
According
to
the

TikTok E-commerce White Paper released by Kalodata, a Chinese data analysis platform, TikTok Shop's US site generated US$14.2 billion in gross merchandise value (GMV) in 2025, an increase of 94 percent over the previous year. Influencers and creators drove about 70.9 percent of sales. This is the new approach in interest-based and emotional e-commerce, where a purchase is the conclusion of a story, not the start of a transaction.

For Chinese sellers, the brand awareness they gain on platforms like TikTok carries over to other platforms as well as offline. Their brand image grown on content-based platforms stimulates growth on Amazon, their own independent sites and even their brick-andmortar retail stores overseas.

A viral hit on TikTok often leads to increased search volume on Amazon, in the same way domestic consumers turn to e-commerce sites like Taobao or JD.com after they see products on Chinese lifestyle apps like RedNote or Douyin.
Content Challenge

Wavytalk's six-second video was not just a stroke of luck, but a result of consistent efforts to produce hit videos. Zou said they started creating content and brand marketing on TikTok in 2022. Later they realized the enormous potential and invested more in video production.

Euhomy, a home icemaker brand, tapped into Americans' passion for iced drinks through scenario-based content. Guo Yiwen, who heads the brand's TikTok operations, told NewsChina that they create ASMR-style videos, featuring close-ups of people crunching on ice. The satisfying sounds trigger an almost visceral pleasure that compels viewers to follow and ultimately buy. "It's a core purchase trigger," Guo said.

However, this new path is not without pitfalls. On platforms like TikTok, sellers face a new environment that involves users of different backgrounds. Many had a rocky start due to cultural misunderstandings.

Cai Fengquan said that Tianyuan Pet learned this the hard way. One of their videos that showed a cat jumping from a height was flooded with comments in the US accusing them of animal abuse. "European and US users are sensitive about luring pets to do dangerous stunts," Cai said. Now every piece of content is vetted by an American reviewer before it is posted for European and US markets.

A viral video can cause an overnight surge in orders, but Chen Yunpeng, a swimsuit manufacturer based in Xingcheng, Liaoning Province, warned that supply chains are not built overnight. "If a video goes viral, you'd better have the goods to ship immediately. Otherwise, even the best content operations are useless," Chen said.

A viral hit is a double-edged sword: It magnifies a brand's strengths, but it can just as quickly expose its weak spots. Unstable supply chains cause supply shortages and if sellers are slow to ship, they get negative reviews. Quality fluctuations can damage the trust of both the content creators the brand hires and consumers.

Cai said that when a dog bed video went viral, their inventory sold out within three days, but it took 45 days to restock. By the time the goods arrived, the buzz had already faded. After that, the team created a dedicated product inventory for TikTok, using localized warehouses to support small-batch, high-frequency restocking instead of the large-scale inventory model used for other platforms.

The low barrier to entry means a hit product will spawn a wave of copycats within days. Zhong Li, who sells squishy toys on cross-border platforms, said that many sellers simply tweak a hit product's design to avoid copyright issues, leading to short product lifecycles and low quality.

In response, he has updated his products using food-grade silicone, finished with a delicate flocking coating (tactile fibers), which are protected by patents and registered trademarks. "We're building a premium brand with strong pricing power," Zhong said.

Meanwhile, competition in this arena is increasingly fierce as the number of shops keep growing. This means more cost to capture traffic, including the commission paid to content creators. New and smaller sellers are facing more pressure as the market has become a winner-takes-all battleground.

On TikTok Shop US, the top 1 percent of sellers generate roughly 60 percent of all sales, while the bottom half of sellers together command only a sliver of the market, according to a survey by New York e-commerce data research firm Marketplace Pulse in June based on nearly 100,000 seller interviews.

Despite the challenges, more are seeing the potential. Zhong Li told NewsChina that the cross-border business park in Hangzhou where his office is located has nearly 100 companies doing cross-border business. The majority of companies are usually run by just two or three people, and they are relatively young. Zhong has been in the park for over a year, and his office has expanded from dozens of square meters to an entire floor.

Sun Peisen, 31, who sells beauty products via content platforms, has grown his team from two to dozens of people in the past two years. His GMV reached 20 million yuan (US$2.94m) in 2025. He told NewsChina that the entry threshold for doing cross-border business is lower now. Building a brand overseas used to mean securing local distribution channels, running ad campaigns, hiring foreign agencies and spending years building a physical retail presence.
