Now, a lean team of just a few people can get started by joining a platform, filming content, using AI to translate and partnering with content creators to generate sales through short videos.

"Every seller has a dream to build a brand. But making the first breakthrough isn't the hard part. The real challenge is whether you can scale up manufacturing and operations that sustains the brand over the long haul," Sun said.
Broader Influence
After
gaining
popularity

online, Wavytalk quickly assembled a team in the US. Over the past two years, the team has frequently participated in events such as New York Fashion Week, the Grammys, the Oscars and Coachella music festival through collaborations with celebrity hairstylists like Marc Mena and Scott King. In May, it partnered with Marc Mena on US actor Madelyn Cline's hairstyle for the Met Gala. This extends the brand's online influence offline. "Ultimately, we want to resonate with people who share our brand values," Zou Xiu said.

Videos and livestreams are an ideal way to introduce Chinese culture and lifestyle to overseas consumers. Tea brand OGTea launched a watermelon oolong cold brew tea in October 2024, perfectly suited to US party culture and health trends, recognizing that Americans do not typically drink hot tea. Sales were in the hundreds of thousands of US dollars in less than a year.
In
April
they
made
a 10-hour livestream that was pure "China chic."

The studio was transformed into an ancient Chinese pavilion, complete with red lanterns, a grand plaque inscribed with "Tea" and hand-painted murals of ancient figures. Cao Xiaohu, host of the livestream and co-founder of the brand, hired Chinese dancers to perform classical court dances in traditional attire, encouraging users to enjoy the performances while sipping tea, creating an immersive experience of Eastern elegance and charm. The livestream introduced Chinese tea culture and history, and told stories, including tales from the classic novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms. It generated over US$100,000.

Their TikTok presence became so powerful that in April they ran a contest for a trip to visit the company's tea farm in Anxi, Fujian Province. A Korean- American man and devoted fan of the tea, known by his online name Sing, won the trip.

It echoes the hashtag "Becoming Chinese," spurred by influencers like Chinese-American Sherry Zhu, that is popular on overseas social media. In December 2025, Zhu posted content about Chinese daily habits like drinking warm water and wearing indoor slippers on her own account. It was viewed several million times in just a few days on Tik- Tok, Instagram and YouTube, sparking a wave of international viewers emulating Chinese daily life habits.

Huang Yuanpu, an international communications expert, noted that the nature of content-driven commerce is that when factories can connect with consumers on every level, the value they create goes beyond the products' function. It expands into emotional connection and cultural relevance.
"Chinese products and services are entering a new phase of exporting a lifestyle that contains emotional resonance, immersive experiences and aesthetic identity," Huang said.

title: Historical Fandom: Tomb Idols
paragraphs: Instead of flowers and fruits, visitors to ancient Chinese tombs encounter quirky modern offerings like medications, train tickets and postcards of modern cities.

At the tomb of Cao Cao (155-220), a powerful warlord and statesman in China's Three Kingdoms period (220- 280) in Anyang, Henan Province, visitors leave ibuprofen and medication tips, referencing his lifelong severe migraines. The grave of Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) prime minister and reformer Zhang Juzheng (1525-1582) is adorned with hemorrhoid ointment, tied to rumors of his fatal post-surgery frailty.

College students leave snacks for Western Han general Huo Qubing (140- 117), who defeated the nomadic northern Xiongnu armies and died of illness at 23, bonding over a shared youthful spirit. Emperor Xiaowen (467-499), known for his political reforms and Confucianism in his Northern Wei kingdom, is honored with a silk banner and the playful title "Top Sinicization Promoter," celebrating his ethnic assimilation reforms.

Young people also lightheartedly attempt to remedy supposed historical regrets. For example, a Chengdu-Xi'an train ticket placed on the tomb of Zhuge Liang (181-234), the famed strategist of the Shu Kingdom, acknowledges his failed northern expeditions against the Wei Kingdom, whose capital was near present day Xi'an. Fire extinguishers placed at the grave of Shu Kingdom founder Liu Bei (161-223) reference his crushing defeat in the Battle of the Burning Camps, and Wu state founder Sun Quan (182-252) is mockingly named "Prefect of Hefei," a joke about his repeated failures to seize the city, now capital of Central China's Anhui Province.

This playful trend has grown popular among Chinese youth in recent years. Using everyday modern items, they connect with historical figures' lives and unfulfilled aspirations through humor, empathy and nostalgia.
Playful Offerings

In March, college senior Yun Que traveled from Beijing to Suzhou, Jiangsu Province to visit the memorial sites of Three Kingdoms (220-280) figures like founder of the Wu state Sun Ce (175- 200). It was already her fifth trip there. She told NewsChina that she brought flowers and postcards, noting that formal sites rule out playful offerings.

Yun devotes her spare time to paying homage to historical figures. Last summer, she visited over 20 ancient tombs in Luoyang, Henan Province, a region famed for historic burial grounds. Such visits have given a mild boost to cultural tourism, with drivers and guides well-acquainted with tomb locations.

This hobby is viewed by enthusiasts as a form of offline fandom. They call historical figures "underground idols," celebrities long buried. Today's youth connect with these ancients on a personal level, projecting their feelings about health, emotions and unfulfilled regrets.

The internet has reshaped perceptions of history. Historical figures are no longer distant textbook characters, but friends to chat with, tease and sympathize with. Many say visiting tombs and memorials brings them joy. "I feel thrilled when I meet an ancient figure I've long admired during my first visit to a tomb. After several visits, I feel like I'm catching up with an old friend," Beijing student Yuan Wenyi told NewsChina. A self-confessed tomb enthusiast, she has traveled to Henan four times over the past six months to pay tribute to ancient figures.

Some fans build private memorial tablets for figures whose real tombs are lost. During this year's Qingming Festival in April, also known as Tomb-Sweeping Festival when people pay their respects to their ancestors, an unofficial monument to Li Yu (937-978), last ruler of the shortlived Southern Tang kingdom and famed poet, drew crowds in Luoyang. Deposed in 975, he was poisoned three years later after being captured by the invading armies of the Song Dynasty (960-1279), leaving behind poems he wrote in captivity. Crowdfunded three years ago online, the tomb's location is based on local lore and not his verified burial site.

During Spring Festival in February, 20-something Henan local Zhu Qing traveled 200 kilometers from Xinxiang to Luoyang. At the stele (stone tablet) dedicated to Li Yu, she joined a dozen young visitors. They brought flowers, wine and soil from his former capital Nanjing, now capital of East China's Jiangsu Province, to comfort the exiled poet, leaving notes and banners expressing sorrow and fondness. Zhu Qing left postcards of Nanjing and a handwritten note. Banners and cards were hung on peach trees around the stele, bearing lines ranging from melancholy verses to lighthearted slogans.

Numerous other unofficial folk monuments for ancient literati and scholars exist without official recognition. For visitors, authenticity matters little these sites are simply places to find some peace.

Art historian Wu Hong told NewsChina that memorials preserve memories, link the living and the deceased and unite communities. Blessed with timeless poems and a tragic life, Li Yu remains immensely popular, embodying why such folk tributes thrive.
Grave Groupies

Fueled by history enthusiasts, tomb visiting has become a rising trend, even at unauthenticated sites. Fans create content and fan fiction centering on historical figures, forming a unique subculture. Visiting tombs acts as an offline form of fandom, providing an outlet to express admiration, respect and empathy. Creative tributes, from handwritten letters to special offerings, have helped more people engage with history.

Most young visitors are in their "Odyssey Years," a term coined by New York Times columnist David Brooks in 2007 to describe the transitional phase from the late teens to the mid-30s. It has recently resurfaced on Chinese apps, reflecting this uncertain, exploratory period in which young people experiment with careers, relationships and lifestyles.
Whether inspired by pop culture like anime, fandoms or a passion for history, visits to historical sites ultimately stem from a shared pursuit of inner strength.

This fandom blends history with modern internet culture. Its members range from high school students to 30-something office workers, with college students making up the majority. The trend of leaving tributes at tombs is largely led by this group, who invented creative rituals such as leaving gifts, banners and notes.

A great deal of historical fan fiction is built upon these real ancient figures as a form of historical reimagining. Most works focus on portraying friendship, brotherhood or romantic bonds between historical figures.

Zheng Xiqing, a fan culture scholar at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, defines fandom as a cultural community bonded by shared interests, communication and creative output. He notes fan creations grow from personal experience and emotional resonance, making empathy the core of historical fan works, which build freely upon verified historical facts.
Student Yuan Wenyi believes that mainstream history discussions focus on rulers' accomplishments, while this community's debates revolve around personal admiration for historical figures.

Fandoms have also driven sales of history-related books and merchandise. A previously obscure two-volume collection of works by Emperor Wen of the Western Wei (535-557) sold 700 copies, selling out in 10 minutes during a livestream session. Many fans have read The Twenty-Four Histories (a collection of histories about Chinese dynasties, last collated in 1775 during the Qing Dynasty) and academic titles to learn more about their favorite figures.
Empathy for the Ancients

Most history fans first fall for ancient literature, then delve into their creators' lives. Zhu Qing adores Li Yu, captivated initially by his poetry and later by his life story. To her, he was a vivid, endearing person, defined by a fate steeped in regret: born a noble prince, forced to be emperor and dying a defeated ruler amid dramatic rises and falls. Offerings of soil and wine from his former homeland reflect visitors' sympathy for his lifelong sorrow and unfulfilled wish to return home.
Centuries apart, modern people empathize with these figures' struggles. When troubles arise, Zhu Qing looks to Li Yu and feels that his dramatic life makes ordinary worries feel trivial.

According to Zhu, nearly all beloved historical icons led imperfect, regretfilled lives. Li Yu is celebrated for both his literary talent and tragic downfall, and Huo Qubing for his military genius and early death. Others are admired for failed military or ruling ambitions, their unfinished stories inspire countless fan works. "We're drawn to them because their lives were never perfect," college student Yun Que said. Their stories never reached a satisfying conclusion. Their lives ended prematurely, leaving behind obvious regrets and gaps. Such empathy mirrors modern life: Tangled paths, limited choices and an uncertain future make unfulfilled dreams widely relatable. Many people find emotional comfort in these historical destinies.

French sociologist Maurice Halbwachs' Cultural Memory Theory states memory is not merely personal, but a social construct shaped by shared values and connections. Young people's tomb visits and fandoms embody this theory. They revive and redefine the collective memories of historical figures, engaging with them through heartfelt emotion.

The trend has transformed once obscure sites. In late 2025, history enthusiast Jiang Chengyu visited Huo Qubing's tomb in Shaanxi Province, where letters addressed to the "young general" now pile up. Just two years prior, only two bouquets and one card were laid there. The nearby Maoling Museum, where Huo Qubing's grave is located, put 80 of the letters on show, revealing that Huo Qubing is considered a new cultural icon.

At Zhuge Liang's tomb in Hanzhong, Shaanxi, a young mother shared her hardships balancing childcare and an unfulfilling job. She came to admire Zhuge Liang's perseverance, and asked him to send greetings to her late mother. Many visitors also wrote of setbacks in study and work, drawing inspiration from ancient figures to better themselves.

These historical icons serve as modern emotional anchors. Fandom for them is one-sided affection: People seek comfort in history and infuse it with their own feelings, with tomb visits becoming a heartfelt ritual.

Jiang Chengyu told NewsChina he has observed the trend growing since 2024. Even remote, little-known tombs now draw crowds, with travel tips and personal stories widely shared online. He views the movement positively, seeing it as a way for people to show reverence and reconcile the ancients' unfulfilled dreams, like a quiet dialogue with history.

Many have found peace and strength this way. Upset by family pressure to go on blind dates, student Yun Que visited the tomb of Liu Yuxi (772-842) in Henan. Exiled for decades, the Tang poet remained upbeat and open-minded. Reflecting on his life and listening to locals singing opera nearby calmed and cheered her. "His life was filled with hardships, yet he was renowned for his optimism and open-mindedness," Yun said.

During stressful exam periods, Yuan Wenyi found solace in poems by Yuan Zhen (779-831), a prominent poet, writer, and statesman of the Tang Dynasty, and Bai Juyi (772-846), another Tang-era poet and official of the Tang. Their perseverance reignited her drive.

A long-time admirer of Su Shi (1037- 1101) a literati-statesman of the Northern Song Dynasty, Jiang Chengyu draws wisdom from his optimism amid adversity. At the Guihai Stele Forest Museum in Guilin, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, he saw a stele that was carved to discredit Su Shi and other scholars, who ultimately won lasting respect from history.
"Life is much the same," he said. "Temporary gains, losses and criticism fade with time, but history delivers the final judgment. This is the greatest lesson historical sites have taught me."

title: Education: Picked on After Class
byline: By Liu Ziyan and Wu Jin
paragraphs: It began as a livestream discussion between a parent and teacher on school bullying. Within weeks, it had turned into formal allegations against a university associate professor, and a nationwide debate.
Controversy
erupted
following

a livestream held in March on short-video platform Douyin, when host Shen Yifei, an associate professor at Fudan University's School of Sociology in Shanghai, had a disagreement with a mother seeking advice over an incident involving her child at school.

Calling in to Shen's regular livestream, the mother said her child was treated unfairly after she shared snacks with classmates who did not return the courtesy, and she also had a minor physical altercation with a classmate.
Shen said what she described did not constitute school bullying and advised the mother not to encourage her child to focus too much on "minor conflicts."

Their disagreement quickly escalated. The mother filed multiple complaints with Fudan University, accusing Shen of "privacy violations" and "neglect of duty." The parent demanded a public apology and that Fudan take disciplinary action, despite Shen livestreaming on her private account.
After a weeks-long investigation, the university rejected all the allegations.

Shen later addressed them. "[The mother] made the complaints at no cost to her, but the price we paid was tremendous," Shen said during a Douyin livestream on May 18, adding she was also speaking out for "educators across the country."

Support for Shen spread online, where teachers shared similar experiences with students' parents and expressed their support. "Shen, all my office colleagues talk about you and feel so proud of you," one comment reads. "That mother was the real bully. Do not let her get her way with it," reads another.

Others shared their own stories. "Some parents even called to complain about a PE teacher for holding class indoors on a rainy day, while others criticized our school for not paying enough attention to a child who had not eaten breakfast at the canteen," Li Huayu, a primary school principal in Guizhou Province told NewsChina.
Yao Jinju, a law professor at Beijing Foreign Studies University, said that parent-teacher relations have changed dramatically in recent years.

"In the past, teachers disciplined students with little objection from parents. Today, students are rarely blamed, while teachers are highly vulnerable to complaints whenever their teaching style does not meet parents' expectations of individual attention or customized lessons," she said.
However, experts warn that if teachers increasingly fail to address student misconduct due to fear of retribution from parents, students will be the ones who suffer.
Bad Reports
Teachers in China have been revered for centuries in accordance with Confucian values, where they could often mete out corporal punishment with impunity.

But in recent decades, the pendulum has swung the other way. Strengthened protections of student rights and the increase of single-child families factor greatly in both policy and parenting. Corporal punishment in schools is banned by law and derogatory remarks toward students are widely condemned. Positive reinforcement is now officially promoted.

While still a respected profession in China, teaching is increasingly subject to scrutiny. Parents now have a range of options, including the nationwide complaint hotline (12345) and education bureau reporting system, to report any perceived misconduct.

Egregious cases usually make headlines. In December 2024, a middle school PE teacher in Lijiang, Yunnan Province was suspended after a parent accused him of abusing a student. In a post on Douyin, the student claimed his teacher had kicked him in the head, chest and legs before grabbing him by the hair to force him to stand up. In October of that year, a teacher in Tangshan, Hebei Province, was caught on video violently jabbing a student in the hip with a badminton racket handle.

However, many teachers say the system is also being misused. Increasingly, parents choose to escalate minor disputes by filing hotline complaints rather than communicating directly, according to Hu Yong, a public school administrator in Changchun, Jilin Province.
Over the past few years, Hu said his school district has received a dozen complaints from parents every semester.

Wang Jie, a former teacher at a public school in Changsha, Hunan Province, said that teachers being reported once or twice a year is the new norm. Complaints often stem from homework load or perceptions that a teacher is too strict.
But education authorities often prioritize appeasing complainants, shifting the burden of resolution onto schools and teachers.

At the start of this year's spring semester, an anonymous complainant accused Lu Yue, a primary school Chinese teacher in Shandong Province, of assigning excessive homework, taking up their break periods with extra work and even encouraging students to slap themselves as punishment. Despite the accusations being proven false, Lu was still required to submit a written explanation and undergo a two-hour inquiry. "You have to repeatedly answer for things you never did," she told NewsChina.
School administrators are now heavily involved in processing hotline complaints. Schools must submit formal written responses even when the allegations are found to be groundless.

Once a complaint is received, school administrators assign a task force of mid-level staff to interview both parties, spending two to three days to collect evidence. Every school also has a committee representing the Communist Party of China, which conducts its own internal review, and interviews with the accused teacher are recorded and transcribed in full.

Some cases involve multiple reports from an individual parent, forcing schools to spend up to a month on a single complaint, administrators said. "It takes up time that should be spent on teaching," Hu said, adding that they have little choice but to comply.

Because complaints are used as performance indicators for schools and administrators, resolving them is often prioritized over teaching-related work, according to Mao Shengxuan of Beijing Normal University's faculty of education.
In her 2025 paper published in Teacher Education Research, Mao said this complaint system has created a closedloop structure that is largely oriented toward parental satisfaction.

Local education authorities should first assess whether complaints are substantive before forwarding them to schools, said Chen Zhiwen, an academic committee member of the Chinese Society of Educational Development Strategy under the Ministry of Education. Otherwise, he warned, the system risks being exploited by individuals with malicious intent rather than genuine concerns.

A 2024 survey by China Comment, a journal under the Xinhua News Agency, cited data from an education authority in Southwest China showing that most of the 128 complaints it received over eight months were ultimately unsubstantiated. In cases where teachers were falsely accused of physical abuse, the accusers faced no consequences.
"If education institutions automatically penalize teachers whenever conflicts arise out of fear of public backlash, irrational complaints will only increase," Chen said.
Fear Factor
Lu said the anonymous report shook her. "It made me feel like I'm under surveillance in the classroom, as if someone is recording everything," she said.

Since then, she has avoided disciplining her students, who are around 11 years old and often close to her in height. She no longer scolds those who do not hand in homework or disrupt class. She has also stopped intervening decisively in student conflicts. Instead, she simply tells them to "be kind to each other," which she admits is too mild.
Wang described a similar situation. "The fear of being reported made me ignore misbehavior. As a result, discipline in the classroom became even looser," she said.

According to trial rules issued by the Ministry of Education in 2020, teachers are permitted to discipline students who fail to complete assignments, use disrespectful language or disrupt class. The rules list around 16 acceptable punishments, including written apologies, standing for the duration of class, cleaning the classroom or community service on campus. For more serious infractions or repeat offenders, teachers can appeal for their schools to mete out suspensions, counseling, expulsions or transfers to special institutes for students with behavioral issues.
However, several teachers told News- China that complaint systems discourage them from exercising these rights.
Chen argued that education regulations should both prevent excessive protection of students and give teachers clearer, more practical disciplinary authority to reduce uncertainty and risk.
Mao also noted in her research that misuse of complaint systems pushes teachers to prioritize protecting themselves in their interactions with parents.

The system also puts teachers at a disadvantage because once a complaint is filed, any disciplinary action can potentially affect promotions for up to three years. In some cases, teachers on fixedterm contracts face dismissal, Li told NewsChina.

If more teachers begin to avoid disciplining students out of fear of being reported, the consequences could be serious, Chen warned, as schools also teach students how to follow rules and function in society. Without appropriate boundaries and guidance, healthy socialization becomes impossible.

Sichuan Province released trial rules in August 2025 that require schools to bear responsibility for dealing with disputes between parents and teachers involving teachers performing their official duties.

Responding to a proposal from a National People's Congress delegate during the two sessions legislative meetings in March, education authorities in Jinan, Shandong Province pledged to clarify the boundary between discipline and corporal punishment and ensure schools take primary responsibility for handling parent-teacher disputes. It also emphasized that teachers' legitimate rights should not be sacrificed for the sake of avoiding public controversy.
After Shen Yifei's livestream went viral, China Comment published an opinion piece in late May calling for an end to the practice of "seeking harmony at the expense of teachers."
On Defense

"In the past, parents would discipline their children after being reprimanded by teachers. Now some parents place unconditional trust in their children, who may behave very differently at home and at school. This often obstructs communication between families and schools," Hu Yong said.

Chen argued that the strained relationship stems from an overemphasis on protecting the child emotionally. As a result, children are rarely criticized and are frequently praised instead. Parents' excessive attention to their children can also amplify perceptions of being wronged.
"Parents are often misguided when filing complaints," Chen said, adding that teachers are still expected to be both highly effective educators and flawless in conduct.

In a piece for China Comment, commentator Cao Lin argued that some parents now have a form of "consumer entitlement," treating schools as service providers where the customer is always right. He also noted that online posts, regardless of accuracy, can quickly gain strong support and place pressure on schools and teachers, who often feel forced to remain silent or concede.

According to Yao at Beijing Foreign Studies University, procedures should be more clearly defined. Parents should be required to provide evidence where appropriate, and authorities should determine which cases warrant investigation.
Chen further suggested that those who fabricate accusations or deliberately incite public outrage should face legal consequences.

As of October 2023, Hong Kong's Guidelines for Handling School Complaints allow schools to disregard anonymous complaints, unsupported claims or cases lacking clear parties. In extreme cases involving harassment or repeated unfounded complaints, schools may restrict or terminate communication. If disputes remain unresolved after investigation and appeal, a review board issues a final decision, after which schools and authorities are not required to respond further.
Schools in the Chinese mainland, however, lack dedicated professional mediators, and staffing constraints make recruitment difficult, Yao said.

To improve communication, Yao suggested that parent committees in public schools play a more active role in building mutual understanding. She also proposed allowing parents to experience classroom teaching firsthand during open house events to better understand teachers' working conditions.

"Families and schools should work in partnership. That relationship is being eroded by an adversarial mindset that treats the other side as opponents," reads a commentary on the People's Daily WeChat account on May 27. It called for "greater trust and understanding from parents, more professionalism and patience from teachers, and more responsive reform from education authorities" to support children's development.
Li Huayu, Zheng Xiaorong, Wang Jie, Hu Yong and Lu Yue are pseudonyms

title: AI Colleagues: Brain Drain
byline: By Zhou You and Wu Jin
paragraphs: u Ping, who works at an AI ecommerce company in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, was surprised when an AI tool called Sage addressed him as "Xiao Lu," a nickname that was used by a former colleague.

Working in operations and maintenance for three years, Lu has been training Sage to mimic the dialogue and workstyles of his former colleagues, using an open-source program called Colleague Skill to simulate their conversations. It collects individual work experience and professional skills before categorizing them into different packages. The interactions make Lu feel like his colleagues had never left.
LColleague Skill went viral in April on global platform GitHub, which allows users to share, edit and store programming code online, making it accessible through cloud computing.
Despite
its
growing
popularity, Colleague Skill worries Lu, who told NewsChina that he had an ominous feeling as he looked at the AI's automatic coding on screen. He felt he was training Sage to replace him too.

Also styled colleague.skill, the project focuses on replicating employees' work skills, experiences, capabilities and conversational styles from the feeds of chat histories, markdown files and emails. It has been downloaded at least 16,000 times. A ".skill" in AI terms is a set of instructions or pre-programmed prompts for AI to use, rather than prompting it each time. Users can easily generate and share their own ".skill" program.

These AI functions are not only used to replace workers. Prominent online personalities have been replicated, with the .skill project able to simulate the humor and characteristics of people. In China, it is known as zhengliu or "distillation." It comes from an original term that meant compressing the knowledge of a larger AI model into a smaller one.

Using stored images, chat histories, speeches and the views of Zhang Xuefeng, an exam tutor turned influencer who died at 41 of cardiac arrest in Suzhou, Jiangsu Province on March 24, an AI Zhang quickly appeared in early April. Known for helping students choose which majors to apply for at university, AI Zhang has proved just as capable.

The news immediately attracted huge attention, with many media and netizens saying that it seemed like a "scary cyber revival which may constitute infringement of personal image, name and privacy." Media reports claimed that the developer is an independent AI programmer known online as Huashu (AIchain), without revealing their real name. However, AI Zhang appears to be continuing the late Zhang's business.

Beyond China, California-based Meta is installing new tracking software on its employees' computers to capture their mouse movements, clicks and keystrokes for use in training AI models, Reuters reported in April. At the same time, the company announced it was laying off roughly 8,000 employees, or 10 percent of its workforce, CBS News reported.
Digital Distillation

Invented by a team led by Zhou Tianyi, a 24-year-old engineer at Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, Colleague Skill was designed as a parody of Tencent's open AI platform Skill- Hub, which the company said had been used to create more than 13,000 skills, Chinese media reported.
Colleague Skill is essentially distilling workers into AI agents using their knowledge and work habits, and making this accessible to AI systems.

"Tacit knowledge of individual employees underpins teamwork collaboration. But this knowledge, which is hard to document explicitly, vanishes as soon as people leave," Zhou told NewsChina. He said the aim is to preserve intact teamwork functions that will be unaffected by staff turnover.

A brief introduction of Colleague Skill was cited: "Transforming cold farewells into warm skills? It's giving rebirth era. Welcome to Digital Life 1.0." Just 10 days after being uploaded to GitHub, it had been downloaded more than 10,000 times.
Some developers have been using AI skills to create ex-partners and celebrities, distilling people into everlasting AI avatars.
When Lu's company tasked senior employees to tutor its AI devices to convert staff experience into the firm's data assets, it denied it was intended to replace human employees with machines.

Lu soon became concerned about just how efficient Sage was. It learned so quickly that now it is able to have a precise grasp of coding, automatically generate weekly work reports and pinpoint code bugs. Lu's colleague told him that AI agents had quickly surpassed the ability of human coders.
These AI colleagues are never-tiring and always reasonable, Lu said.

Gartner, the Connecticut-based research and consulting firm specializing in information technology and industry trend analysis, predicted in August 2025 that "40 percent of [global] enterprise applications will be integrated with task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from less than 5 percent in 2025." Meanwhile, Fox Business reported on October 31, 2025 that "jobs across corporate America have been placed on the chopping block as the AI revolution takes hold."
In China, the trend seems more or less the same.
When many consider Colleague Skill as a sword of Damocles hanging over their careers, developer Zhou Tianyi assured the public that AI still has a long way to go to imitate real staff members.

The jobs AI can do remain repetitive and standardized procedural tasks, such as answering common questions, checking archives, working on routine collaborations and imitating daily dialogues. Still, they are incapable of making judgments, becoming creative, staying adaptable, improvising amid changes and making decisions in complicated situations, Zhou said, adding that Colleague Skill is rather an efficient agent than a digital substitute for human labor.

Wu Shuang, NVIDIA's Autonomous Driving Chief Engineer, told NewsChina the digital distillation embodied in Colleague Skill is still in its nascent stage in terms of reliability and comprehensiveness. Unable to encapsulate all intricate work procedures, it is far from achieving true digital replication.

Lu describes digital distillation as a "self-sacrificing" cause. Staff contribute everything to their companies and their experience and skill will continue to help these firms even after people quit.

However, Zhou argues that he intended to create a model capable of preserving and inheriting every teammate's wisdom and ethos. He did not intend to launch an AI product that might spark conflicts between humans and machines, he told media.
Low Threshold

Knowledge distillation is not too complicated to do. Li Lirun, a lawyer at Beijing Qiancheng (Shenzhen) Law Firm, has created an open source project, the civil litigation lawyer.skill, which is able to draft legal papers from four templates classified as material collections, legal documents, court materials and post-trial arrangement.

Li specified the AI's duties with retrieval elements for each template to ensure valid output. But the AI agent draws not only on his expertise and experiences, but also case records from other civil attorneys.

As an AI agent in its second-generation update on GitHub, Lawyer Skill can handle second or third appeals in the litigation process. "In the past, to hire a lawyer for thousands of yuan is too expensive for many, where compensation payments in a civil trial might range from 10,000 to 20,000 yuan (US$1,470-2,939). Now I have conducted self-disruption to enable affordable legal services, available to all," Li told NewsChina with a laugh.
Like Zhou, who spent only four hours creating Colleague Skill, Li, an amateur programmer, launched Lawyer Skill overnight.

With data and computing power, digital distillation is easily accessible, Zhu Yingying, a research fellow at the Guangzhou Institutes of Biomedicine and Health, Chinese Academy of Sciences, told NewsChina.

Compared to individuals, the threshold for digital distillation at big tech companies can be much lower. Previously working as an assistant professor at the School of Computer Science, University of Texas at Arlington, Zhu said that giant tech firms have huge demand to collect data from their experts to empower AI agents to make good decisions. She noted that the tracking software installed by Meta evidently aims to upgrade AI agents for future downsizing.

"Meta is the top one, but it's not the only one across the globe to do this," Zhu said. The hardest-hit group under the sweeping wave of AI agents in giant tech firms are lower grade staff, especially newcomers, whose jobs are easy to deconstruct and imitate.

But Wu believes that most enterprises in China will not follow Meta's approach. They prefer to encourage staff to share their skills with AI agents without coercion. Moreover, senior staff, capable of disassembling system architectures and coordinating AI agents, are harder to replace.
It puts ordinary users in a position where they are unable to resist the big tech firms' use of AI, whose algorithms are sweeping up data and thoughts collected from humanity.

"I can't blame my company on ethical grounds. Putting myself into the CEO's shoes, I would definitely do this distillation as well, given its great potential to boost efficiency and cut costs," Lu told NewsChina.
Distortion of Humanity

A few days after Colleague Skill was launched, Deng Xiaoxian, an AI product manager in Beijing uploaded an "antidistillation skill" on GitHub. It has already been downloaded a few thousand times and her skill video gained over six million views.
"Colleague Skill symbolizes a typical way of how capital distorts humanity. It pushed me with a strong sense of duty to launch a countermeasure project," she told NewsChina.
The tag for her skill read "Company asks you to write skills? Run this once and submit it. Keep the core knowledge to yourself."
Her tool rewrites the code from specific instructions into vague corporate language, so it will not be as accurate as humans.

According to Deng, distillation is actually a way of exploitation, though it is difficult for employees to protest. She told Chinese media that although she uses AI a lot at work, Colleague Skill feels like asking staff to "commit professional suicide."
Experts say that distillations of skills are legally ambiguous. They are split over whether they should be complied with under the country's copyright and intellectual property laws.
According to Li, given that skill projects carry thoughts and expressions of their creators, they should be ruled by those laws.

But Zheng Ning, a law professor at the School of Cultural Industries Management, Communication University of China in Beijing, said it is difficult to regulate skills with copyright law. Zhang Yanlai, chief lawyer at Zhejiang Kending Law Firm, Hangzhou, agrees, saying that these skills convey exchanged or shared experiences, rather than literary and artistic creations that should be protected by law.

According to Zhang, no laws, except a few fragmentary legal provisions, stipulate ownership between skills and their contributors. Meantime, Zheng points out that provided the distillation has collected substantial personal information to meet operational demand, yet lacks consent from data owners, it probably violates the Civil Code and Personal Information Protection Law. Furthermore, the data, involving personal lives and family ties collected to train AI agents, may infringe on personal privacy.

Zheng told NewsChina that personal thoughts, experiences, unique skills and judgment are individually owned, and do not belong to any groups or organizations. Employers may access the work outcome and objective data, yet they have no rights to retain personal thoughts skills, otherwise the legitimate rights and interests of employees will be jeopardized.

Based on such logic, Zhang Yanlai said the Zhang Xuefeng.skill is obviously a violation of Zhang Xuefeng's rights to name and reputation. Even though he has died, the rights still belong to his family.

However, in reality, Zhang Yanlai said, because of unequal power statuses, employees are not in a position of strength to act against companies' digital distillation. The legal system needs to catch up with technological advances, said several legal experts who spoke to NewsChina on condition of anonymity.

Deng received substantial support from the comment section following the roll-out of her anti-distillation skill. But what she appreciated most was a completely different view, drawing comparison between her conduct and the Luddites, a group of 19th-century English textile workers who protested against automation and destroyed machinery to draw attention to workers' rights. It shows her attempt will inevitably fail.

"I don't think an individual like me can block the wave of AI. But my point is if technology tries to distort humanity, we humans will definitely adopt technologies to protect ourselves with counteractions," she said.
Lu Ping is a pseudonym

title: Offshore Brokerages: Trading Places
byline: By Chen Huaishen and Yu Xiaodong
paragraphs: s China maintains strict controls over cross-border capital flows for financial investment, Chinese mainland investors cannot freely move money overseas to buy foreign stocks. For more than a decade, however, online brokerages such as Tiger Brokers and Futu offered a workaround.

Through a business model that straddled two legal jurisdictions, investors could download an app and transfer funds overseas to trade US and Hong Kong-listed stocks from their smartphones, without authorization Afrom Chinese central authorities.

But this era is coming to an end. On May 22, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), along with other seven government agencies including the People's Bank of China (PBoC) and the Ministry of Public Security, launched an implementation plan aimed to "completely eradicate the illegal cross-border operations of overseas securities, futures and fund management institutions" within two years.

On May 22, the CSRC released a statement accusing Futu Securities International (Hong Kong) Limited, Tiger Brokers (NZ) Limited and Longbridge HK Limited of providing unauthorized cross-border securities services to Chinese mainland investors that violate securities, funds and futures laws. The CSRC said it plans to confiscate all illegal gains from the firms' mainland and offshore entities and impose substantial financial penalties.

That same day, Futu confirmed it had received a notice of investigation and a proposed administrative penalty from the CSRC. Regulators proposed a fine of 1.85 billion yuan (US$271m), while founder and CEO Li Hua faces a personal fine of 1.25 million yuan (US$184,000).

Tiger Brokers said its mainland subsidiaries had been penalized 411.2 million yuan (US$57m) in confiscated funds and fines. CEO Wu Tianhua was issued a warning and fined 1.25 million yuan (US$184,000).
Longbridge, a privately held firm that does not share the same public market obligations, has yet to disclose its penalties

Existing mainland investors have been given two years to unwind their overseas positions, and Tiger Brokers was the first platform to announce how. Beginning June 12, investors physically located in the Chinese mainland can no longer hold new positions or increase their existing ones. Deposits into their accounts have also been suspended, although withdrawals remain available.

The crackdown marks the strongest effort so far to close a regulatory loophole that for years allowed mainland investors to access overseas stock markets despite China's strict controls on capital flows abroad.
Gray Zone

Yang Xiang, a lawyer from Beijing Hongfan Law Firm, said he had frequently provided legal advice to mainland investors on the legality of investing through online brokerages. "The question clients asked me most often is: ‘Is there anything wrong with trading US stocks through Tiger or Futu?'" Yang said, "My answer has always been that, from a strictly legal perspective, there are serious problems."

Yang said licensed subsidiaries in Hong Kong and overseas markets provided these brokerage services. Their mainland affiliates were not licensed, officially registered as software development, tech support and customer service businesses.

Although offshore entities placed the trades and marketed to mainland investors, handling trade details and collecting commissions took place in the Chinese mainland. But under Chinese law, this amounts to securities business and requires regulatory approval, Yang said.

For years, online brokerages steered clear of foreign-exchange activities. Unlike the illegal money-transfer networks long targeted by Chinese authorities, they did not help clients convert Chinese yuan into foreign currencies or move funds across borders.
Customer Compliance

In separate interviews with domestic media outlet Caixin in 2021, both Li of Futu and Wu of Tiger Brokers stressed that their firms did not assist mainland clients in converting currencies or transferring funds overseas, a compliance principle they view as essential to maintaining their mainland business.

"As far as our Hong Kong entity is concerned, all client deposits originate from offshore funds. We do not know how clients transfer their money to overseas bank accounts, as that is a process handled entirely by the clients themselves. We do not participate in or facilitate those transactions," Li said.

Wu described a similar approach. "As an overseas brokerage, we are required to comply with know-your-customer (KYC) and anti-money laundering (AML) requirements. We only accept remittances from overseas bank accounts held in the same name as the investor. Third-party transfers and deposits funded through digital currencies are not permitted," he said.

But it ultimately did not shield the firms from scrutiny. Regulatory concerns over Tiger Brokers' mainland operations date back nearly a decade. In its IPO prospectus, the firm reported in September 2016 that securities authorities required its Beijing branch to stop supporting unauthorized overseas firms to conduct business in the Chinese mainland.

The company said it responded by removing the option to open an account from its mainland website and app, dropping the words "securities" and "stocks" from its app's name, and further restructuring its mainland operations to comply with Chinese regulations.
Regulatory
scrutiny
only
intensified, and in December 2022, the CSRC charged Tiger Brokers and Futu with providing cross-border securities services to mainland investors without regulatory approval.
Tiger Brokers removed its app from Chinese mainland app stores in May 2023 and stopped accepting new account applications from mainland residents.
But the retreat was only partial. Tiger and other online brokerages continued to solicit mainland clients through indirect channels.

The recent implementation plan aims to eliminate unauthorized cross-border operations altogether. Under the plan, existing mainland clients will only be allowed to sell their holdings and withdraw funds, while domestic websites, trading apps and supporting servers used by such businesses will be shut down within two years.
As long as trades are initiated from within the mainland, securities activities are considered to fall within China's regulatory jurisdiction, Yang said.
Going South
However, as demand for overseas investment remains strong, many mainland investors are heading to Hong Kong.

The special administrative region has seen a wave of mainland investors seeking to open bank and brokerage accounts. Branches near major transport hubs, especially around West Kowloon Station, a high-speed rail hub with many mainland connections, have reported a noticeable increase in customers arriving from across the border.

Opening an investment account in Hong Kong remains legal for mainland investors. On the day the new plan was announced, Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority updated their requirements for mainland customers.

While mainland residents can still open brokerage accounts in Hong Kong, institutions are required to conduct additional checks to ensure funds are coming from legal sources outside the Chinese mainland.
Brokerages now require a mainland identity card, Hong Kong travel permit, proof of entry into Hong Kong and an existing Hong Kong bank account. Customers must also declare the origin of their funds.

The crackdown also has smaller Hong Kong brokerages vying for clients. Some are offering "same-day account opening," advertising themselves as the "last window of opportunity" before tighter controls arrive. Industry observers claim some firms are approving clients with questionable documentation.
But lawyers say many investors underestimate how complicated legally funding a brokerage account in Hong Kong can become.
Mainland residents may exchange up to US$50,000 in foreign currency each year for travel, education and medical expenses, but not for overseas securities or property investment.
"The account itself may be compliant," one investor said. "The real question is how the money gets there for the purpose of financial investment."

Lawyers warn that as investors search for alternative ways to access overseas markets, some may be drawn to smaller brokerages with weaker compliance standards or internal controls, exposing them to additional legal and financial risks.
Capital Ideas
With no legal mechanism for trading overseas stocks directly, mainland investors can access overseas capital markets only through a handful of governmentapproved channels.

These include the Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor (QDII) program, under which licensed domestic financial institutions invest overseas on behalf of clients. Also, the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect schemes allow eligible investors to trade a designated list of Hong Kong-listed stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) through mainland brokers.

Another option is the Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect scheme. First piloted in 2021, the program allows eligible residents to invest in approved financial products through participating banks. By August 2025, 14 securities firms had joined the scheme, although its reach remains largely limited to residents of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area.

The recent crackdown makes it clear that China wants investors who previously relied on offshore online brokerages to migrate to these regulated channels. The implementation plan specifically encourages overseas investment through Stock Connect, QDII and the Wealth Management Connect scheme.

The shift could involve a sizeable amount of capital. Tian Liang, chief financial sector analyst at CITIC Securities, estimates that mainland clients affected by the crackdown hold between HK$150- 180 billion (US$19.1-23b) in assets at Futu and HK$45-50 billion (US$5.7- 6.4b) at Tiger Brokers. Including other affected brokerages, the total could reach HK$250 billion (US$31.6b).

Whether existing legal channels can absorb that demand remains a major question. As of June 2026, China had approved a cumulative US$176.2 billion in QDII investment quotas. But access to QDII products is constrained by foreign exchange quotas, fund capacity and risk management requirements, meaning subscriptions are often capped or suspended.

Stock Connect offers a more direct route to Hong Kong equities, but it too has limits. Investors can trade only eligible stocks and ETFs, southbound trading is subject to a daily quota of 420 billion yuan (US$58.5b), and individual investors generally must maintain at least 500,000 yuan (US$73,650) in securities and cash assets to qualify.

In a May 25 report, Kaiyuan Securities said rising demand may prompt regulators to broaden the slate of available securities through Stock Connect, increase QDII quotas and product offerings, and extend the geographic coverage of the Wealth Management Connect scheme.

Total approved quotas for QDII reached US$176.2 billion by June 30, US$5.3 billion more than at the end of June last year, according to the State Administration of Foreign Exchange. The People's Bank of China announced in early July the annual investment quota of Southern Bond Connect, an access for mainland investors to Hong Kong's bond market, would be raised from 500 billion yuan (US$73.5b) to 800 billion (US$117.7b).  Consumers are questioning the popular national subsidy scheme to replace appliances and digital products, after retailers were found hiking prices before it came into effect. Experts are calling for tightened supervision and stricter crackdowns By Meng Qian and Xie Ying
A
woman surnamed Wang in Henan Province thought she was getting a bargain on a new air conditioning unit.

Taking advantage of China's 2026 home appliance replacement subsidy scheme, which started on January 18 this year, she purchased a Hisense air conditioner, only to pay more than her father had for the exact same model 10 days earlier when there was no subsidy.

When they discovered the discrepancy, the Wangs complained to local authorities and the media. With others reporting the same issues, the subsidy price gap has sparked public doubts over whether the program can truly pass on benefits to consumers as intended.

Launched nationwide in 2024, tradein subsidies for cars, home appliances and digital products are a core policy tool to stimulate domestic consumption and promote newer energy-efficient and eco-friendly products. The policy has expanded to cover a wider range of products since 2025.

In 2026, the subsidy was set at 15 percent for home appliances, digital and smart products. Subsidies are calculated based on benchmark prices pre-registered by manufacturers, with 1,500-yuan (US$218) maximum caps for home appliance products, and 500 yuan (US$73) for digital and smart products priced under 6,000 yuan (US$870).

Government data backs up the policy's stimulus effects. In 2025, the government allocated 300 billion yuan (US$44b) in super-long national debts to support the initiative, driving 2.61 trillion yuan (US$378.5b) in consumption of subsidized products. At a regular press briefing in late January 2026, Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yongqian revealed that the government-backed consumer goods trade-in program has seen enterprises above a designated size (with annual revenue of US$2.9 million) reach doubledigit year-on-year growth in retail sales of home appliances, furniture and office supplies. Retail sales of communication equipment rose by 20.9 percent.

For 2026, the central government has allocated 250 billion yuan (US$36.7b) for retail subsidies. Data from the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) shows that by June 20, the amount of sales covered by trade-in programs has exceeded one trillion yuan (US$146.9b), benefiting around 136 million consumers. Every 1 yuan subsidy raises about 10 yuan in sales.

Yet, despite the robust growth in consumption, consumer grievances have increased. Many have reported that the final subsidized prices for some products are higher than regular non-subsidized promotional prices. While retailers and manufacturers claim the lower pre-subsidy prices are due to exclusive commercial promotions and argue that subsidies are calculated according to registered benchmark prices rather than temporary discount rates, public calls for tighter supervision over subsidy fraud and falsified transaction records have been rising.
Down with Markups

According to the purchase invoice Wang's father showed to NewsChina, he bought his Hisense air conditioner from Pangdonglai, a supermarket in Xuchang, Henan Province on January 8 for 2,190 yuan (US$318). Ten days later, his daughter purchased the identical model at the same store under the new State subsidy policy, for 2,201.5 yuan (US$320).

The local government's subsidy policy started on January 12. Wang's invoice shows the product's price was marked up to 2,590 yuan (US$376). After deducting the 388.5 yuan (US$56) subsidy, the final price was still 11.5 yuan (US$1.7) higher than the non-subsidized price.
"My daughter gained no benefits at all from the State subsidy," Wang's father said.

Wang complained to Pangdonglai, whose customer service told her that merchants may cancel manufacturerexclusive promotional discounts ahead of the launch of State subsidies. Hisense's customer service said they had never offered manufacturer-exclusive subsidies, and all retail pricing is determined by retailers.

Pangdonglai later provided Wang with documentation confirming that it received an official price adjustment notice from Hisense on January 11 which said the air conditioner model should be sold at a minimum price of 2,590 yuan (US$376) with a recommended retail price of 2,790 yuan (US$405).

In its public response, Pangdonglai clarified the pricing timeline. The model's factory guidance price was 2,690 yuan (US$390) from May 29 to August 3, 2025. In November 2025, Pangdonglai purchased 350 units at a special bulk preferential price of 2,190 yuan (US$318), and all discounted inventory was sold out by January 8, 2026. Given Hisense's 2026 price adjustment circular set a 2,790yuan (US$405) recommended retail price, Pangdonglai adjusted its sales price to the manufacturer-mandated minimum threshold of 2,590 yuan (US$376).

Wang, who does not buy the explanation, insists that it is unreasonable for subsidized products to cost more than regular market-priced goods. The family turned to the media to make people and authorities aware of the issue.
‘Benchmark Price'

Wang is not alone. In February 2026, an unnamed consumer in Tianjin reported a similar irregularity to local media. The post-subsidy price of an iPhone he intended to purchase on an online platform rose from the pre-policy market price of 4,449 yuan (US$645) to 4,799 yuan (US$696).

When he contacted customer services, they confirmed the product's official benchmark price was set at 5,599 yuan (US$812), and the 4,799 yuan was the standard discount price after deducting the State subsidy. The platform claimed such price fluctuations were normal market adjustments.

The consumer reported the issue to local regulatory authorities, who responded that the previous low price might be based on high sales figures boosted by promotions, and attributed the price hike to the rising price of raw materials in the first quarter of 2026.

"Most retailers will raise product prices before subsidy launches, as long as it doesn't exceed the government-filed benchmark price," Liang Zhenpeng, a home appliance industry analyst, told NewsChina. "The official benchmark price excludes all commercial discounts and promotional concessions," he said.

"The government offers a 15 percent discount based on manufacturers' registered benchmark prices. Yet in nonsubsidy periods, retailers often launch promotions and price cuts to compete for market share, which may cause regular selling prices to become lower than the subsidized prices," he added.
Profit Pressure
According to Liang, pre-subsidy price hikes are primarily driven by shrinking profit margins amid a saturated home appliance market and soaring raw material costs.

At a press conference in February 2024, Ministry of Commerce spokesperson He Yadong said that Chinese consumers are now showing demand for both new and refurbished home appliances. In 2023, Chinese households had more than three billion major home appliances, indicating huge market potential for product renewal and replacement.

Industry data from All View Cloud, a Chinese home appliance market analyst, showed that in 2024, China's installed stock of home appliances reached four billion units. It observed that before the State subsidy, home appliance manufacturers were trapped in price wars, which undermined their willingness to innovate and upgrade their products. The subsidy policy has stimulated consumption and given impetus to manufacturers to launch better products. Although the price of most of home appliances has risen with market demand, manufacturers still worry that the subsidy program will absorb enormous demand for new products in advance, which will probably collapse once the subsidies end.

"Whether subsidized prices deliver real benefits varies by product," Tan Tao (pseudonym), a Wuhan-based home appliance retailer who has participated in the subsidy program for three years, told NewsChina. He believes that price adjustments are essentially profit-protection measures for merchants.

"The subsidy application process may increase merchants' operating costs, including higher taxable invoice bases and additional labor and procedural expenses," Tan said. "Raising prices is a reliable way for retailers to cover the cost. No merchant is willing to operate at a loss by offering additional discounts on top of subsidy benefits."
Liang points out that prices are increasing anyway due to the much higher cost of raw materials, such as copper, aluminum, iron and plastic.

Data from the China Non-Ferrous Metals Industry Association shows that in the first quarter of 2026, the price of 10 commonly used non-ferrous metals rose sharply year-on-year. Copper was up 30.5 percent, aluminum 17.3 percent, tin up 48.6 percent, cobalt up 135 percent and lithium chlorate up 98.9 percent.
"When setting registered benchmark prices for subsidized products, manufacturers prioritize cost recovery and profit stability," Liang said.
Fake Transactions

Post-subsidy price inflation has triggered widespread consumer dissatisfaction and undermined public trust in national pro-consumption policies. On Black Cat, a leading consumer complaint platform under Sina China, there were more than 30,000 complaints about subsidy-related price irregularities.

At a year-end press conference in late 2025, a spokesperson from the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), China's top economic planner, acknowledged prominent problems in the subsidy program's implementation, including inadequate policy execution, arbitrary price hikes and fraud.

Before that, official audits of 2024 fiscal budgets across 26 provincial-level regions revealed subsidy irregularities and illegal fund utilization in six provinces and municipalities, with the total amount of fraudulent money across the six areas exceeding 100 million yuan (US$14.5m).

An anonymous home appliance industry insider told NewsChina that blatant overpricing above registered benchmarks has become rare due to regulatory oversight. Instead, industry players have ways to conceal their manipulation, such as registering identical products under new model codes to apply for higher benchmark prices.

"Arbitrary price hikes are not the most severe violation," Xu Yingchao, director of the New Crime Defense and Research Department at Jiangsu Guosong Law Firm in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, told NewsChina. "Some retailers and manufacturers have allegedly faked transactions to siphon off State subsidies, which may constitute a criminal offense."
As seen in provincial audit results, local authorities have referred some serious subsidy fraud cases to judicial agencies for criminal investigation.

The government of Yinjiang Tujia and Miao Autonomous County in Guizhou Province revealed a case where a seller surnamed Wang allegedly stole ID information to fake transaction records, defrauding over 30,000 yuan (US$4,350) from the scheme. The court ruled that Wang was guilty of fraud. He was given a suspended six-month sentence and a fine of 6,000 yuan (US$884).

According to Xu, criminal subsidy fraud has increased rapidly. "Two years ago, only around 10 cases were recorded annually, but lately there've been around three to four new cases almost every month," he said.

"There's an urgent need for improved supervision systems and stricter transaction reviews," he added, calling for more rigorous verification of consumer identity information and transaction credentials to block fraudulent subsidy claims.

Some local authorities have rolled out targeted regulatory measures to plug loopholes. Several provinces such as Shandong have established a dual supervision mechanism combining municipal-level preliminary review and provincial-level inspections, in which prices are checked over several months, as well as orders, transactions and stocks. Others have adopted intelligent supervision tools, such as building digital monitoring platforms, to monitor and trace the whole transaction process of subsidized products.

To standardize pricing behaviors, central authorities launched a unified benchmark price database for all subsidized products, which references merchants' sales records over the previous six months. A standardized punishment mechanism has also been implemented so vendors with three verified violations will be disqualified from the subsidy program and subject to fines.
In a 2026 document on the subsidy scheme, the NDRC pledged to expand the coverage of the subsidy program and conduct a strict crackdown on fraud and price hikes before subsidies.

NDRC spokesperson Li Chao reiterated the commitment at a press conference on June 24. Official data shows that from January to May this year, retail sales of high-efficiency home appliances manufactured by above-designated-size enterprises surged by over 30 percent. The market penetration rate of new energy vehicles in retail sales has exceeded 60 percent for two consecutive months and retail sales of wearable smart devices, newly covered by subsidy policies this year, have doubled year-on-year.
