The explosive growth of AI-generated shows resembling live action has shaken China's multi-billion-yuan microdrama industry. Studios sit idle, while performers and content creators are struggling to find their roles - and engage audiences burned out on AI slop By Wang Shihan and Ni Wei
ormer actor Zhang Xiaolei was busy in his greenhouse when our reporter texted. "I've just finished picking chili peppers and now I'm packing them. Let's talk later," he texted back.

Wearing thick cotton gloves, the 28-year-old rushes to harvest thousands of kilograms of peppers in June before packing them for delivery. Just a few months earlier, he had been wearing tailored suits and playing domineering CEOs in hit microdramas.
"Now, I'm a domineering farmer," he joked.

Over the past three years, Zhang appeared in nearly 200 microdramas. He comes from a dancing background, and worked his way through minor roles to Flanding CEO leads in female-oriented romance dramas. His day rate eventually hit 6,000 yuan (US$884).

But after this year's Spring Festival in February, acting opportunities seemed to suddenly dry up. This change coincided with the launch of Seedance 2.0, ByteDance's AI video generation model, which dramatically improved AI video quality.
Between February and April, Zhang got just one role, and for one-third his previous rate. Disillusioned, he returned to his hometown in Northwest China's Qinghai Province to farm full time.
This year, countless microdrama actors like Zhang have been struggling to find work in microdramas. The major reason is AI-generated productions disrupting the entire industry.

Some 33,000 microdramas were released in all of 2025, according to the National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA). In Q1 2026 alone, about 128,000 microdramas were released, 95 percent of which were AI-generated, said the China Online Audiovisual Association.
Cast Away
As one internet user put it, "AI's first blow falls on the actors."

During the boom years for live-action microdramas between 2023 and 2025, Zhang was based in Xi'an, Shaanxi Province, one of China's three major production hubs, alongside Hengdian in Zhejiang Province and Zhengzhou in Henan Province.

To play wealthy CEOs, Zhang bought inexpensive suits because actors were expected to provide their own wardrobe. "I was constantly kneeling for scenes, so my suits wore out quickly," he told NewsChina. "I couldn't afford expensive ones."

The entire industry was operating at breakneck speed, and microdrama actors worked grueling schedules. Zhang once filmed for three consecutive days with almost no sleep, grabbing only brief naps in taxis between locations. Production crews routinely stocked sets with coffee, energy drinks and even nitroglycerin tablets in case someone suffered a heart attack. He once saw a lead actress collapse during filming and be rushed to hospital.
But Zhang sensed that something had changed in February. Just before filming was due to begin on a new production, he was told it had been canceled.

"They simply pulled the plug," Zhang said. "The director even tried to shorten the schedule by a day to save the project, but it didn't work. Everything stopped so suddenly that most people had no idea what was happening."

That same week, Seedance 2.0 launched on February 12, and microdrama platforms were soon tightening their belts. For many smaller production teams, the previously guaranteed funding of 200,000-300,000 yuan (US$29,400-44,200) for greenlit projects disappeared.
The industry panicked to reposition itself. Some production companies are paying actors up to several thousand yuan for the rights to digitally reproduce their faces for AI use.

One actor who requested anonymity told NewsChina that productions now rely almost entirely on AI-generated backgrounds. Human performers appear only to deliver a few lines, while "background extras are barely needed anymore."

Over the past two and a half years, Wu Weibin, a 39-year-old actor at Hengdian World Studios in Zhejiang, appeared in more than 100 microdramas. Often cast in patriarch roles, he became known as the "King of Hengdian Dads."
But his kingdom has severely shrunk. "I couldn't land a single role," Wu said. "Everything fell apart."
He contacted assistant directors, agents and fellow actors of his generation, only to discover they were facing the same reality.
"My hardships reflect the agony we're all enduring industry wide," he said.

Other Hengdian extras told NewsChina that more than 100 actors now compete for a single minor role, such as an imperial eunuch. In just three years, Hengdian has gone from the country's busiest microdrama production hub to empty soundstages. Tens of thousands of actors remain there, waiting for auditions that never come.
Left Reeling
The first day on his new job, Yao Guoli was handed a script and assigned to direct an AI production.

Yao had previously produced live-action microdramas in Xi'an. Early in the year, he accepted an offer from a leading production company. Eight days later, he was informed his would-be department had been dissolved.
The only offer left came from a new AI-based studio making animated dramas. "After seeing where the industry was heading, I decided to switch to AI," Yao told NewsChina.

Now instead of coordinating actors, equipment and locations, Yao sits at a workstation with multiple AI tools. His work involves converting scripts into storyboards, collaborating with artists to generate dozens of 15-second AI video clips and handing them over to editors for assembly.

The microdrama market peaked at over 100 billion yuan (US$14.7b) in 2025, with viewership reaching nearly 700 million, according to the NRTA. Around 137,000 actors registered with the Hengdian World Studios Actors Guild, nine times the number of the previous year.
Much of that boom was driven by a generous incentive model: Platforms opened their script libraries to independent studios to pick and choose which to shoot, guaranteeing them up to 350,000 yuan
for
completed productions.
Yao said the model allowed production companies to increase profit margins by controlling costs, which fueled industry expansion.

But that changed in early January, when platforms cut their minimum guarantees. Suddenly, many studios were facing uncertain revenue streams, suspended orders and canceled productions. This lines up with AI-generated dramas entering the picture.

AI live-action microdrama Zhan Xian Tai (Execution Ground for Immortals) surpassed 100 million views within six days of its release in January. According to tech media outlet Blue Whale Technology, the project only required a crew of 12 and around 100,000 yuan (US$14,700) in computing costs over a 30-day production period, roughly one-quarter of the total budget for a similar live-action microdrama production.

Yang Miao, president of Xi'an Qiuyuan Pictures, one of China's leading microdrama studios, said the company fully restructured in March, cutting its staff of around 200 by half. Those who remain work in both live-action and AI productions.

Yang said a live-action microdrama typically costs 600,000-1 million yuan (US$88,300-147,100) and takes more than a month to complete. By comparison, an AI production can be finished in 10 to 15 days for just 80,000 to 100,000 yuan (US$11,800-14,700).

But so far, lower costs have not translated into higher profits. "We might earn up to 400,000 yuan (US$58,850) from producing three AI dramas in a month," Yang said. "Previously, a single liveaction drama could generate 700,000- 800,000 yuan (US$103,100-110,500)."
Animated
AI
drama
production peaked in March 2026. According to DataEye, about 180,000 AI dramas were streaming across major platforms by March, including roughly 50,000 new releases that month alone.
"Animated AI dramas are currently the easiest and fastest field for ordinary creators to transition into," Zhou Tong, head of an AI drama studio in Henan Province, told NewsChina.

Notably, the vast majority of this year's AI productions are animated, which are not only cheaper to make but cheaper to watch. Looking at the top 100 paid titles on microdrama platform Hongguo, animated AI productions average between 0.5-1 yuan (US$0.07-0.14) per episode. according to industry tracker DataEye. By comparison, AI-generated live-action series are priced similarly to traditional microdramas, between 0.8-2 yuan (US$0.10-0.28), but usually require lower budgets.

Although AI-generated productions now account for most new releases, they have yet to win over mainstream audiences. According to the NFTA, liveaction productions accounted for only about one-fiftieth of new releases during the 2026 Spring Festival period but drew 25 times more viewers than AI dramas.

Industry data from DataEye paints a similar picture. By the end of February, more than 127,000 AI dramas were available online, but fewer than 150 had gotten more than 100 million views, just over 0.1 percent of the total hitting this benchmark.
Face Off
One viewer who regularly watches both live-action and AI microdramas told NewsChina she is growing increasingly frustrated with AI productions.

"Every lead character looks the same. They all seem to come from the same template," she said. "Their digital faces lack the subtlety and vitality of real actors. Most of the storylines are repetitive and lack originality."

As celebrities are increasingly litigating against unauthorized AI face cloning, most producers rely on models available in AI libraries. But because these are often limited to around 100 faces, many productions end up with similar-looking characters.
The viewer said that female protagonists often wear the same outfit throughout an entire series, while characters move stiffly and unnaturally.
Yao said these shortcomings largely stem from cost cutting.
"Technical
imperfections
can
be fixed," he said. "But every revision costs money. When budgets are tight, producers assume audiences will tolerate a certain level of imperfection."

He added that AI productions with larger budgets (costing more than 1,500 yuan (US$220) per minute) can already achieve near-photorealistic results, but much of the market consists of low budget productions costing as little as 100 yuan (US$14) per minute.

"Audience tolerance varies by genre," Cao Yanzhong, founder of Youhe Culture, a microdrama production company, told NewsChina. "Viewers of male-oriented fantasy dramas, such as dragon lord or war god stories, care more about fast-paced plots and are more forgiving of technical flaws. Audiences for palace intrigue and romance dramas, which mostly comprise women, pay much closer attention to visual details."

Yao believes AI has weakened the bond between audiences and creators, hurting emotional engagement. "When viewers watch a live-action drama, they appreciate the performances and recognize the effort behind the production," he said. "With AI dramas, their first instinct is to look for signs if it's AI-generated and point out imperfections."
This focus on the technology makes it much harder to build an emotional connection.
"AI dramas need much stronger storytelling and emotional hooks," Yao said. "Only then will audiences become immersed enough to forget they're watching AI-generated content."

In April, several major platforms launched campaigns targeting lowquality AI productions. On June 25, the NRTA issued new guidelines introducing a tiered regulatory system for AI microdramas. Productions with budgets exceeding 800,000 yuan (US$117,700), or those involving sensitive topics such as politics, diplomacy and national security, will face stricter oversight than smaller productions.
Zhou believes tighter regulation and stricter platform review will encourage studios to put quality over sheer volume.
"Once low-quality productions are filtered out, the AI drama industry will return to a healthier path of development," he said.
Despite the recent production boom, Zhou believes public acceptance of AIgenerated dramas will take much longer.

"Audiences won't embrace AI content overnight," he said. "Just as many successful animated film franchises took more than a decade to gain wider acceptance, AI dramas will also need time to mature." Former CCTV anchor turned cultural advocate argues that the longevity of traditional crafts lies not only in commerce and creativity, but also in their power as mindful,
everyday practices that elevate the human experience
FBy Yi Ziyi

or most Chinese audiences, Zhao Pu is remembered as one of the country's most recognizable television news anchors. But after leaving China Central Television (CCTV) in 2015, he turned his attention to a lifelong passion: protecting and revitalizing China's traditional handicrafts and intangible cultural heritage (ICH).

Zhao has founded organizations promoting traditional crafts, produced documentaries and written extensively on artisans. This year, he founded the World Craft Forum, an online platform that promotes ICH academic and cultural exchange worldwide.

In an interview with NewsChina, Zhao discusses the forces that are reshaping the future of traditional craftsmanship, and why crafts survive by being used, not by being preserved in museums or through subsidies alone.
NewsChina: What first sparked your interest in traditional handicrafts?

Zhao Pu: This passion did not emerge out of nowhere. Its origins lie in my birthplace and upbringing. I was born in Anhui Province and raised in Huizhou (in southern Anhui), a uniquely fertile cultural region.

In old Huizhou, even ordinary farmers farmed the land by day and practiced calligraphy at night. People's reverence for learning was ingrained in the local identity. Huizhou is known for its heritage of the "Four Treasures of the Study": Hui ink, Xuan paper, Xuan brushes and She inkstones (Xuan and She come from ancient prefecture names in southern Anhui). They were the heart of every ancient scholar's study.

Raised in this calligraphic culture, I naturally became familiar with traditional handicrafts. The drive to revisit history and engage with traditional culture is invariably tied to one's formative background. This is undeniable, and it explains my decades-long commitment to the protection and promotion of ICH.
NC: When did preserving ICH become more than a personal interest?

ZP: It was back in 2003 when I was working at Beijing Television. I produced and directed a short documentary series titled Inheritors. The documentary centers on two core themes: ICH inheritors and the challenges many traditional practices face today.

Take Yangliuqing New Year woodblock prints (Yangliuqing is a town in Tianjin). They were once an indispensable part of Chinese New Year rituals. In the old days, setting off firecrackers, gathering the whole family to eat dumplings and pasting door gods on gateways were household traditions. As these agrarian New Year customs gradually faded from daily life, the paintings struggled to survive. Without the cultural soil that once sustained them, the craft lost its foundation, leaving no successors to carry it forward.

Another example is movable-type printing in Rui'an, Zhejiang Province. Today, movable-type printing has long lost its practical function as a means of transmitting information and retains only cultural value. Information has gone fully digital, rendering physical printing blocks obsolete.
NC: How did your work in television help you promote traditional crafts and ICH?
ZP: Once I joined television, especially after becoming a CCTV host with considerable public influence, I clearly recognized the immense power of modern media for cultural preservation.

In the early days, Sina Weibo did not exist, and blogs dominated online platforms. I maintained a blog on 163. com and published two widely discussed articles. The first exposed the neglected and filthy state of Qi Baishi's (1864-1957) tomb (in western Beijing), disgracing the master painter's legacy and exposing failures in cultural relic protection.

The second article had an even greater impact. Titled "Preserve the Soul of Old Beijing," it focused on the former residence of renowned architects Liang Sicheng (1901-1972) and Lin Huiyin (1904-1955) on East Zongbu Hutong. Real estate developers planned to demolish the couple's previous home, coining the phrase "protective demolition." But how can demolition coexist with preservation?

The article drew the attention of (artist and cultural scholar) Feng Jicai. He rallied multiple members of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference to campaign for the residence's preservation, yet it could not be saved. (It was demolished in 2012.)
Back then, I lacked the authority to use official media resources for cultural preservation, so my personal blog worked as an early form of social media.
NC: You often place traditional crafts in a broader historical and cultural context. Why is that perspective important?
ZP: Yes indeed. For decades, I have made a habit of evaluating each phase of my work against a broader historical timeline.
My
long-standing
dedication

to ICH stems from a process of cultural self-reflection: What cultural influences shaped our generation of Chinese people, and where do our civilizational roots lie? That is only the first layer of my reflection. A deeper question remains: Where will Chinese people, carrying this legacy of traditional culture, go in the future?
Although my work appears to document the past, my gaze is firmly fixed on the future, as I continually examine how traditional culture can coexist with modern society.

Ten years ago, I formulated three guiding principles for ICH preservation. First, trade is the best form of protection. For craftsmen to sustain their livelihoods and pass down their skills, their work must sell. Second, use is the best form of inheritance. Crafts endure only when they are integrated into daily life, and those disconnected from practical life will eventually disappear. Third, sharing is the best form of dissemination. People willingly share the beauty of traditional crafts only when they truly value them.
NC: You've argued that the market offers the best protection for traditional crafts. What do you mean by that?

ZP: Crafts isolated from market feedback cannot endure in the long term. Market feedback has two forms: one is positive consumer recognition, a willingness to purchase that incentivizes craftspeople, while critical feedback on flawed materials or design pushes artisans to refine their work. This creates a positive feedback loop.

Relying solely on government subsidies is akin to raising seedlings in a greenhouse: Once funding ceases, the project collapses. Revitalization does not rely on one-sided government financial support. It requires deep market integration and self-sustaining commercial cycles.
The
internet
and

livestreaming are the most accessible channels for promotion and sales today. I have hosted livestreams myself, selling kesi (cut-silk tapestries), cloud gauze and agarwood (a rare resinous wood used for carving and fragrances) and silk handicrafts. Nevertheless, during economic downturns, consumers cut spending on such ornamental items first.

Online promotion carries inherent drawbacks: Most skilled artisans excel at crafts but lack the skills for livestream sales. Established artisans now form specialized teams to do livestreams. For instance, master sculptor Zhu Bingren (inventor of the molten copper art technique with a museum in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province) lets his son handle the commercial side of his work. Short videos and livestreaming are the essential communication tools which have become impossible for artisans to avoid.

Offline cultural events serve as another key commercial channel, with Suzhou Bense Fair and Wenzhou Qingdeng Fair as industry benchmarks. Nevertheless, the commercial influence of fairs is limited and, in the meantime, is on the decline, affected by the current economic situation.

Digital platforms boast lower barriers to entry: Anyone with a smartphone can film craft production processes and share them on the internet. A rural craftsman who goes by Shanbai, a 25-year-old man from rural Hunan Province, went viral for videos of him making pipa (traditional stringed instruments) and stoneware.
NC: What does the Guochao trend - Chinese fashion that blends traditional culture with modern style - tell us about young people's relationship with traditional culture?
ZP: From my perspective, Guochao is a cultural and commercial movement in which young consumers make purchases based on historical narratives disseminated through mass media.

For instance, the surge of tourists wearing Hanfu (traditional Han clothing) at the Palace Museum (in Beijing) stems not from young people studying history, but from television dramas set in the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) that have sparked audiences' imagination. Consumer demand for Hanfu and traditional cultural and creative products reflects young people's desire to seek out their cultural roots. Young people embracing traditional culture is a positive and encouraging trend, far preferable to cultural indifference and disconnection.
NC: China's ICH catalogue has expanded rapidly in recent years, even to include some food products. Has the definition of ICH become too broad?

ZP: China operates a four-tier ICH catalogue system: county-level, municipal, provincial and national, with stricter review criteria the higher the tier. County-level standards remain the most lenient, which is the primary reason behind the overexpansion of ICH categories.

Three things are fueling this: The ICH label boosts value for cultural tourism development, catalogued projects qualify for government subsidies and registered ICHs serve as cultural performance metrics for local governments.

Scholars opposed classifying foodrelated practices as ICH. Cuisine survives through natural market selection, popular flavors endure across generations without formal catalogue protection. Yet as the catalogue system expands nationwide, standards are set by local cultural and tourism bureaus, with overarching guidance documents issued by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.

Many local governments prioritize the sheer number of ICH listings, recklessly expanding catalogues with lax standards. However, the tiered filtering system self-regulates: County-level projects rarely advance to municipal, provincial or national rosters. In the long run, fading public interest and dwindling subsidies will reduce lowvalue listings.
NC: Many local governments are using ICH-themed events to promote tourism, but some have struggled with planning and execution. What lessons should they learn?

ZP: This exemplifies the typical pitfalls of State-administered cultural projects. Local governments aim to build tourism brands and attract visitors, yet often lack robust crowd forecasting and security planning, leading to a lose-lose predicament. Huge public funds are expended, but last-minute cancelations harm public trust.

Even economically developed regions in the Yangtze River Delta suffer from planning oversights, not to mention smaller cities. I have always believed market-driven initiatives should remain in the hands of the market, with minimal administrative intervention. Commercial events self-adjust according to visitor flow and revenue, while topdown government planning often lacks accurate demand forecasting, resulting in a waste of resources.

Huizhou fish lanterns, for example, survive through scenic cultural tourism events. Without commercial applications, they would only appear sporadically during village festivals, risking eventual extinction. Fortunately, modern media amplifies tourism appeal for such practices, and the open market offers the most sustainable path forward.
NC: What role do you think traditional crafts will play in the age of AI?

ZP: The widespread adoption of AI has amplified the value of traditional handcrafts. Anyone using AI tools will notice that machine-generated work lacks a distinct human touch. The beauty unique to humanity lies in imperfection: Handmade pieces inevitably bear minor irregularities, which embody vivid human texture. High-precision machinery eliminates all imperfections, sacrificing this unique aesthetic quality.
The rapid development of AI has sparked a global existential question: How do we define human value? As intellectuals, we must redefine the contemporary significance of traditional crafts and ICH.

Yanagi Soetsu (1889-1961), a master of modern Japanese craft aesthetics, established the theoretical framework of "the beauty of Mingei." Mingei does not refer to precious ceremonial artifacts enshrined in temples, but the inherent beauty of ordinary, affordable objects used in daily life. He pioneered the hugely influential concept of "the beauty of daily use."

Few Chinese scholars have elevated folk handicrafts to the level of aesthetic philosophy as Yanagi did. Most scholarship remains confined to surface-level technical analysis of artifacts, while Yanagi's work penetrates the metaphysical Dao.

During exchanges at the World Craft Forum, I aim to build consensus among international scholars on philosophical and ethical grounds. The shared anxiety triggered by AI unites researchers worldwide in exploring a single question: How will humanity navigate the AI revolution?

I have one prediction concerning the role of traditional crafts: In the future, ICH and traditional crafts will evolve into spiritual practices similar to yoga. Yoga is a practice for physical conditioning and mindful breathing.
Traditional handicrafts will become a secular, everyday spiritual practice, similar to meditation, allowing humanity to converse with its history, calm the mind and perceive the passage of time.

title: Opera: Acts of Humanity
byline: By Dai Menglan and Zhao Jingyi
paragraphs: an a centuries-old art form continue to captivate audiences in the AI era?

For Hong Kong director Fredric Mao Chun-fai, the answer lies in reimagining tradition. His latest Cantonese opera, To Be or Not to Be - The Legendary Story of Lu Wenlong, which premiered in Hong Kong in June as a joint Hong Kong-Shenzhen production, revisits a classic tale through a contemporary lens.

The son of a Song Dynasty (960- 1279) general, Lu's parents were killed in a battle with the invading northern rival Jin Dynasty (1115-1234). He was taken in by the Jin army commander, only to eventually struggle with remaining loyal to his adoptive Jin father or to his homeland.

Rather than focusing solely on battlefield heroics, the production explores its protagonist's inner conflict, moral choices and search for identity, while pairing traditional Cantonese opera with modern stage aesthetics.

The production reflects Mao's longstanding approach to theater. Throughout his career, he has blended traditional Chinese performing arts with contemporary storytelling and theatrical techniques, while preserving their cultural essence.

A veteran dramatist, director and educator, Mao has spent decades bridging CChinese and Western theater. Among his triumphs is New Love in a Fallen City (2006), a musical adapted from Eileen Chang's classic novel of the same name that tells a tangled love story set against the wartime collapse of Hong Kong.
After performing on Broadway and leading the Hong Kong Repertory Theater as its first artistic director, he has become one of Hong Kong's most influential advocates for innovation in Cantonese opera.

In an interview with China News Service, Mao discusses how Cantonese opera can remain relevant to modern audiences, Hong Kong's role as a cultural bridge between China and the world, and why human creativity will remain irreplaceable in the age of AI.
CNS: Your new Cantonese opera To Be or Not to Be - The Legendary Story of Lu Wenlong explores patriotism and heroism. What do you hope modern audiences will take from it?

MC: The classic tale of Lu Wenlong has long been performed in Cantonese opera and many other forms of Chinese opera. Our new production, viewed through a modern lens, explores how the protagonist discovers his true self and defines what kind of hero he wants to be amid conflict and moral dilemmas.
It also reflects my understanding of Chinese theater today: besides telling a compelling story, opera should inspire audiences to think deeply.

According to The Great Learning, one of the Four Books of Confucianism: "The purpose of great learning lies in manifesting a virtuous character and cultivating people to pursue the ultimate good." I hope this opera conveys that a hero's conscience, values and moral character are what matter most.
CNS: What first inspired your passion for theater?
MC: I have been fascinated with Chinese theater since childhood. I was born in Shanghai and moved to Hong Kong when I was 10.

While living in Shanghai, I watched traditional Chinese operas performed by renowned masters, including Peking Opera master Zhou Xinfang, who portrayed Prime Minister Wang and Bao Zheng in the classic opera Qin Xianglian. Both Shanghai Yue Opera and Cantonese opera left a profound impression on me and nurtured my lifelong passion for traditional theater.

In the late 1960s, I earned a master's in theater arts in the US. My first professional stage performance was in 1971 at the Berkeley Repertory Theater in California. I worked with the Napa Valley Theater Company between 1972 and 1976, first as an actor and later as a director. I also served as artistic director of the company. From 1983 to 1984, I served as deputy director of the New Asian American Theater in New York. These experiences greatly shaped my teaching and creative work after I returned to Hong Kong.
In 1980, renowned playwright Cao Yu [Wan Jiabao] visited the US, where Columbia University staged an Englishlanguage production of his play Peking Man in his honor.

I was fortunate to perform in the production. Through expressing Chinese cultural heritage on stage, my performance won praise from both Chinese and Western media. I realized that this stemmed from my deep-rooted Chinese cultural identity, and the production marked the pinnacle of my acting career.

Two years later, I visited the Chinese mainland as a representative of the New Dramatists [a nonprofit incubator for emerging playwrights based in New York], where I met theater professionals in Beijing, Wuhan and Shanghai to better understand the future direction of Chinese theater. Soon afterward, I received an invitation to teach in Hong Kong and decided to return to my cultural roots.
CNS: As Hong Kong seeks to brand itself as an international hub for cultural exchange, where does theater come into play?

MC: The Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts, Hong Kong's first professional performing arts institution, was founded in 1984 and officially opened in 1985. I was honored to serve as head of acting at its School of Theater and helped design its curriculum.

Hong Kong theater has a unique advantage: it brings together Chinese and Western cultures while maintaining strong local characteristics. Although I gained valuable experience in the US, I knew we could not simply copy the American training system. Teaching must be tailored to local students. Rather than focusing heavily on theory, I often used sensory training and improvisational exercises to help students understand and apply theatrical skills. It is equally important that young performers stay rooted in their own culture.

Adapting and staging translated plays is another strength of Hong Kong theater because the city can quickly absorb and reinterpret the essence of Western theater. The central government expects Hong Kong to become a hub for cultural and artistic exchanges between China and the world, and we should fully leverage this advantage while embracing the present era.

Hong Kong needs to cultivate its own cultural identity by integrating Eastern and Western traditions. Young people, many of whom have had limited exposure to traditional Chinese culture, should deepen their understanding of that heritage while incorporating the best elements of Western theater. Hong Kong theater should preserve its local identity, inherit Chinese cultural traditions, and serve as a bridge between Chinese and foreign cultures.
CNS: You have brought local productions to audiences on the Chinese mainland and overseas. What does Chinese theater need to succeed internationally?

MC: The original musical Sweet and Sour Hong Kong (2003), which I coproduced and directed, blends Broadway style with Hong Kong characteristics. I invited two legendary Hong Kong musicians, James Wong (Wong Jum-sum, 1941-2004) and Joseph Koo (Koo Kar-fai, 1931-2023) to compose the music, while adapting the script from renowned playwright He Jiping's One Moon, Not Two Homelands. Its performances in Shanghai gave Chinese mainland audiences an opportunity to experience Hong Kong musical theater.

When directing New Love in a Fallen City (2006), I created the roles of a storyteller and a singer to reflect on and interpret the story, echoing the inner thoughts of the protagonist Bai Liusu while expressing my own understanding of Chang's original novel. The production also showcases both Hong Kong and Shanghai cultural characteristics.

We were invited to perform New Love in a Fallen City at the See You in Beijing Art Festival in 2006. During the first half of the performance, the audience remained completely silent, which made the cast very nervous. We worried that Beijing audiences did not appreciate the production, unlike the enthusiastic reception we had received in Hong Kong and Shanghai. However, when the curtain fell, the audience responded with warm applause. I believe their silence reflected how deeply absorbed they were in the performance.
Chinese theater faces many challenges in going global, but the effort is worthwhile. The key is to identify our unique cultural identity and integrate it into our productions.
CNS: You have devoted many years to revitalizing Cantonese opera. How can theater continue to preserve its human spirit in the age of AI?

MC: Cantonese opera is inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Although it enjoys support from the Hong Kong government and a loyal audience, it still suffers from insufficient innovation and repetitive productions. That is why I have focused on researching and revitalizing Cantonese opera in recent years.

Funded by the Hong Kong Jockey Club, my adapted version of Pavilion of a Hundred Flowers (a traditional Cantonese opera set in the Yuan Dynasty (1271- 1368) about love and political intrigue) was staged at two consecutive Hong Kong Arts Festivals and later toured the Chinese mainland. Its success demonstrates that audiences have both an appetite and demand for innovative interpretations of traditional opera.

AI certainly poses challenges to theatrical creation. In recent years, some productions have mechanically incorporated fashionable new elements. When performers simply execute fixed requirements, they risk losing their individuality and becoming replaceable by AI. Theater is a collaborative art, and a performer's interpretation lies at its heart. AI can deliver standardized and programmed performances, but it can never replicate theater's true soul: the unique artistic insight of creators and performers, and the emotional connection forged through live interaction with audiences.

Young theater artists should learn from both Eastern and Western traditions in a thoughtful and rational way, rather than blindly imitating either one. Innovation must be rooted in tradition. Only by preserving the essence of traditional Chinese culture can we maintain our cultural identity and confidence. True innovation is not about piling on fashionable elements, but about revitalizing enduring traditions through modern perspectives and creative techniques to expand the possibilities of performance.
This article was originally published by W.E. TALK, a China News Service production. Reprinted with permission from CNS

title: Exhibition: Gilded Child
paragraphs: he National Museum of China is transporting visitors back more than 1,400 years with "Discoveries at Li Jingxun's Tomb - A Glimpse into 6th- 7th Century China."

The exhibition, which began in April and lasts until October 8, draws on burial artifacts and historical documents discovered from the tomb of a young girl from the Sui Dynasty (581-618), which reunified China after nearly 300 years of division and laid the foundations for the subsequent flourishing of the Tang Dynasty (618-907).

The exhibited treasures, including gold and silver ware, jade artifacts, glassware, silk textiles and exquisite jewelry that blend Persian and Central Asian artistry, offer far more than a Tglimpse into the poignant life story of a child.

They open a unique window into the broader cultural landscape of 6th-7th century China, a cosmopolitan age when the Silk Road brought Persian gold and silver, Indian jewelry and Central Asian craftsmen to the heart of the Middle Kingdom.
Grave Curse
In 1957, while conducting archaeological excavations to accommodate construction to the west of Xi'an, Northwest China's Shaanxi Province, archaeologists discovered a wellpreserved Sui tomb.
Having never been looted, its clear structural layout and abundant items remained intact, making it the highest-ranking and best quality Sui tomb discovered to date.

Oriented north to south, the tomb passage extends into a burial chamber, where an outer stone coffin sits in its center. Inside rests a palace-shaped inner stone coffin. The structure is laid out with an order and precision that reflects the Sui ritual system.

Even senior archaeologists were awed by the sheer richness and splendor of the tomb's items. But nothing prepared them for the hair-raising characters carved onto the inner stone coffin: "Whoever opens this shall die."

According to the epitaph, the tomb belonged to Li Jingxun, whose courtesy name Xiaohai, means "little one." She was born in the year 600 and died in 608. The very name "little one" speaks to how cherished she was.

Li Jingxun was born with a silver spoon in her mouth. Her lineage extended across the Northern Zhou (557- 581) and Sui dynasties, positioning her family at the heart of the Guanlong Military Aristocracy, a marriage-based, multi-ethnic group of warrior elites. Deeply rooted in Northwest China, the group held sway over the region while China remained splintered between rival northern and southern powers.

As a direct heir to this legacy, Li Jingxun's bloodlines were intimately woven into the imperial houses of both the Northern Zhou and Sui dynasties. Her paternal great-grandfather was Li Xian, a grand general of cavalry for the Northern Zhou. Her maternal grandfather was Yuwen Yun, Emperor Xuan of the Northern Zhou. Her maternal grandmother, Yang Lihua, was not only an empress of the Northern Zhou but also the eldest daughter of Yang Jian, otherwise known as founding Emperor Wen of the Sui.
The Li, Yuwen and Yang families, all converging in this one young girl, drove the wheels of history forward during the tumultuous transition from the Northern Zhou to Sui.
The Little One

The chilling characters carved on the stone coffin, "Whoever opens it shall die," are at once a curse against tomb raiders and an everlasting protection, embodying the most eternal determination of a grandmother for her young granddaughter taken too soon.

That grandmother was Yang Lihua, born in 561, who raised Li Jingxun personally, bestowing upon this granddaughter all the tenderness she had never been able to give her own daughter or herself. Apart from the curse, the epitaph on the tomb reads that Li Jingxun was cherished and tenderly raised solely by her grandmother Yang Lihua.

The epitaph offers no glimpse into Li Jingxun's childhood days, yet from the sheer opulence of her tomb and its curse, we can piece together a vivid picture: She wore the finest silks, was adorned with the rarest jewels, and spent eight years sheltered beneath her grandmother's loving wings. Some modern writers have described her as the "most spoiled child in history."
Grandmother's Love

Throughout her life, Yang Lihua found herself trapped in a relentless power struggle. Her father, Yang Jian, was a senior minister in the Northern Zhou Dynasty. From a young age, Yang Lihua was renowned for her beauty, noble bearing and gentle disposition. At 13 years old, she was selected as crown princess to crown prince Yuwen Yun. Five years later, Yuwen Yun ascended the throne as Emperor Xuan, and Yang Lihua was named Empress Tianyuan. Their daughter Princess Yuwen Eying, born at an unknown date, was the mother of Li Jingxun.

Two years later in 580, Emperor Xuan died of illness, and 20-year-old Yang Lihua was honored as empress dowager. To ensure political stability, she appointed her father Yang Jian as grand counselor and commander of all military affairs, effectively placing the military and political power of the Northern Zhou in his hands. Yet only seven months later, her father initiated a move that thrust her into an impossible position. Yang Jian deposed the Northern Zhou emperor, proclaimed himself emperor and changed the dynasty's name to Sui.

After the fall of the Northern Zhou, Yang Lihua became Princess Leping of the Sui. As a woman who had been an empress of the Northern Zhou, she was now the daughter of the man who had destroyed her adopted dynasty. Torn between her birth family and her marital family, she endured a lifetime of unresolved conflict.

As the only figure from the former dynasty to remain active within the Sui imperial family, Yang Lihua still held a certain influence over the Northern Zhou's former subjects. But she stayed away from court politics and isolated herself from any political alliance. Her only solace was perhaps her daughter and her granddaughter.

Yang Lihua's love for Li Jingxun was more than a grandmother's devotion. It was a quiet act of self-redemption. She had never truly lived. So she poured into Li Jingxun everything life had denied her.

However, in 608, a sudden illness claimed Li Jingxun's life. That glimmer of light was extinguished. All of Yang Lihua's obsession was transformed into opulent burial rituals and protective curses. She would use every means possible to keep her "little one" close and safeguard her forever.

One year later, Yang Lihua accompanied her younger brother, Emperor Yang of the Sui on a western inspection tour. By June, they had reached Zhangye, in modern-day Gansu Province, where Yang Lihua passed away at the age of 49.
Gold and Glass

According to the ritual system of the Sui Dynasty, underage children could not be interred in a family's ancestral cemetery or accompanied by lavish grave goods. However, Yang Lihua was determined to give her little girl a dignified final resting place. She chose a burial site within Wanshan Nunnery in the Sui capital and had a magnificent multi-story Buddhist pagoda built over the tomb.

Wanshan Nunnery was once Yang Lihua's own residence, making it a place of profound personal connection. By choosing this nunnery as her granddaughter's final resting place, the grandmother ensured the child would remain perpetually by her side, where she could offer protection and solace.

Li Jingxun's tomb followed the full ritual standards of an adult noblewoman. The number and exquisite quality of the burial goods surpassed those found in many tombs of adult Sui Dynasty aristocrats. The more than 230 extraordinarily luxurious objects include gold and silver ware, jade artifacts, ceramics, glassware, silk textiles and jewelry, each a masterpiece of Sui Dynasty craftsmanship.

In the exhibition at the National Museum of China, a gold hairpin is at the center. It features a lotus-leafshaped base made of rolled gold sheets, on which stands a moth woven from fine gold wire. The eyes of the moth are inlaid with pearls, its antennae are made of gold wire, and its hollow body could possibly hold incense. Beneath the moth cluster a six-petal gold flower and triangular gold leaves. The flower stamens are set with pearls and gemstones. As the wearer walks, the ornament gently quivers. In ancient times, wearing such hair ornaments was an important custom during the Lantern Festival, which marks the end of Chinese New Year.

Another highlight is a gold necklace inlaid with pearls and gems, measuring 43 centimeters in length and weighing 91.25 grams. The top of the necklace is adorned by a deep blue lapis lazuli with an intaglio-carved horned deer. At the lower end, 24 pearls surround a single chicken-blood stone, and beneath it hangs a heart-shaped sapphire measuring 3.1 centimeters in length. The gold necklace blends Persian and Central Asian artistic styles. Its techniques, patterns and materials can all be traced back to regions such as Afghanistan or Pakistan. It is likely that the necklace was an imported object brought to China via the Silk Road, or made by a Sogdian craftsman living in China. Alongside the gold necklace, a pair of gold bracelets was unearthed. The bracelets are oval-shaped and divided into four sections, each section wider at the ends and inlaid with gems. This type of gold bracelet is unparalleled in ancient Chinese history, with its design likely originating in Northern India.

Glass used to be one of the most exquisite and expensive materials. Before the Sui Dynasty, glassware originating from Sassanian Persia had flowed into China. Archaeologists discovered eight glass artifacts and some glass beads in Li Jingxun's tomb, including a green glass jar with a lid and a small green glass bottle.

These burial artifacts ensure that Li Jingxun could still enjoy a refined and happy life in another world. Although she only lived eight years, a fleeting breath in the long march of dynasties, she managed to cross time through her grandmother's love.

title: Hangzhou: Heady Brew
paragraphs: Even after living in China for almost nine years, I still have a bucket list of the country's most iconic places. So, what better place to start ticking them off than a true cradle of Chinese civilization? Long dubbed "paradise on earth," Hangzhou, in East China's Zhejiang Province has served as a muse for generations of artists and scholars, anchoring a history that traces back over five millennia. I knew it would be beautiful. But it wasn't until I finally stood on the banks of West Lake that I truly understood why travelers have been drawn here for centuries.

For a long time, history books claimed that Chinese civilization began solely in the Yellow River basin to the north. However, the discovery of the Liangzhu ruins in Hangzhou completely changed that narrative. Because of Liangzhu, UNESCO and international historians now recognize that Chinese civilization started 5,000 years ago. This established the Yangtze River Delta as a major, foundational birthplace of the culture.

Setting off from Beijing South Railway station, I grabbed some snacks and settled in for the 4.5-hour highspeed train to the city's center. Before I knew it, I was exiting the train and heading to my first stop: the Grand Canal Museum.
A Grand Canal

To really understand how this ancient civilization came to life, I wanted to see how a single, man-made waterway could shape the destiny of an entire nation. The museum does an incredible job of breaking this down using interactive areas and stunning historical detail. The real highlight for me was slipping on a pair of the VR glasses you can pick up upon entry. When you scan QR codes in front of an exhibit, you are transported into ancient life along the waterway. I left feeling like I had personally journeyed through time from the origin of the canal to how it is used today.

While the Grand Canal Museum uses VR to show you the past, walking down Hefang Street lets you step right into it. This bustling pedestrian lane was the commercial heart of Hangzhou back when it was the capital of the Southern Song Dynasty (1127-1279). Today, it's a sensory overload of old-world charm. I could smell the sweet aroma of osmanthus cakes mixed with the scent of traditional Chinese medicine halls. There were artisans and performers dressed in traditional clothes, making bread and hammering intricate jewelry exactly the way it was done centuries ago. But, I got even more excited when I saw the lane of food trucks offering delicious snacks and matcha ice cream.
After diving into thousands of years of history, I chose to stay at the Narada Resort, located in the Liangzhu Cultural Village, about 20 kilometers outside the center.

The next morning, I set out for Jingshan Temple, a historic Zen Buddhist site hidden deep in the forested mountains of Hangzhou's Yuhang District. Getting there by car is quite easy. It's just a scenic, one-hour drive from downtown. However, to keep the mountain pristine, outside private vehicles aren't allowed to drive all the way up to the temple itself.

Instead, you park at the visitor lot at the base of the mountain, where you have a choice: embark on a steep, roughly 3-kilometer hike along the ancient stone trail or catch the scenic shuttle tram. Wanting to save my energy for exploring the grounds, I opted for the tram, which is completely free! You just scan a quick QR code at the visitor center or the lot to grab a digital ticket, hop on, and ride it up. The actual entry ticket to the temple itself is 30 yuan (US$4), which includes three complimentary sticks of incense. The winding ride up through the bamboo-forested mountains was incredibly beautiful, but nothing compared to the moment the temple itself came into view.

Once I got closer, the scent of incense filled the air. The temple has various rooms to visit, including the main hall housing a grand statue of Sakyamuni Buddha, as well as three famous historic iron Buddhas dating back to the Song Dynasty (960-1279). While I was there, I was lucky enough to see a ceremony being performed by the monks. Watching them pray and show gratitude while everyone stood completely still was a moving moment. The temple grounds also offer interactive experiences where you can try your hand at traditional tea whisking, or you can head over to a scenic overlook to get a perfect shot of the mountains. I decided to save the tea whisking for later, though, because I had already made an appointment to join a ceremonial tea whisking class in Jingshan Village.

In Jingshan Village, the class dives deep into the ancient history of tea whisking, a tradition that peaked over 1,000 years ago during the Song Dynasty. This isn't your average coffee house latte swirl. It's an ancient art form where matcha paste is used to create intricate designs in the foam, mirroring the style of traditional Chinese inkwash paintings. The most famous local brew is the iconic Longjing tea, grown on terraces around the city.

First, we were given a green tea powder to mix with hot water. Then, using a traditional bamboo bristled whisk, we were told to use a vigorous, rhythmic motion to froth it up to the perfect consistency. Once you achieve the desired thick foam, you use a special slender bamboo stick to dip into a darker matcha paste and gently draw your design onto the surface. Inspired by my morning journey up the mountain to the temple, I decided to try a scene of a bamboo forest and mountains, which gave me a lot more respect for the talent of these artists.
Lake Legends

Saving the best for last, I spent my final day exploring the iconic West Lake. Walking along the pathways, the swaying willows framed against the backdrop of the water and open lily pads was breathtaking. As you stroll, you pass historic stone bridges and see a striking gold water buffalo sculpture called Jinniu Chushui, emerging from the shallows, a nod to an ancient Han Dynasty (206 BCE- 220 CE) legend where a mythical golden ox would rise to spew water and save the city from drought.

Out on the water, traditional wooden sculling boats glide peacefully across the lake. You can pay to hop on one of these boats, which offer a perfect vantage point of the historic temples and pagodas, like Leifeng Pagoda. Looking out over that timeless landscape, it was easy to see exactly why this place inspired iconic poets and scholars like Bai Juyi and Su Dongpo, who spent their lives trying to capture its beauty.
Even when famous explorer Marco Polo visited centuries ago, he declared that Hangzhou was "beyond dispute the finest and the noblest city in the world." And I agree.

If you want to get lost in China's ancient history, Hangzhou is a must-visit. Trust me, whether you're looking for ancient history, tech-driven museum exhibits or just a tranquil retreat into nature, Hangzhou has it all.
Practicalities

Hangzhou is a one-hour quick train ride from Shanghai, and offers convenient connections to other nearby cities, including Suzhou, Nanjing and Ningbo. The city has an international airport, and a comprehensive metro and bus system, as well as ride share bikes. ABy Sam Duckett

s the summer holidays roll around, my mom is also preparing for a three-week trip to Beijing. While I'm sure she's excited to see her son and granddaughter, I suspect she has a secondary motive this year: escaping the intense summer heat that has settled over Europe.
And on that note, let's do the most British thing imaginable and talk about the weather.

While England has been grappling with one of its hottest summers in recent memory, Beijing has been surprisingly cool. Rain has rolled in every few days, keeping June's average daytime high at around 25 degrees Celsius. Although temperatures have edged up as summer progresses, it feels noticeably milder than previous years.

Instead, we've been living through a rather odd balancing act. The weather swings between pleasantly cool and absolutely pouring with rain. Just when it starts to feel like summer has finally arrived, another heavy downpour appears and resets everything.

I'm certainly not complaining. The cooler temperatures have made family outings far more enjoyable, especially with a young daughter in tow. But adjusting to the regular rain has taken a little getting used to. A few practical purchases quickly found their way to the top of my shopping list: lightweight raincoats, wellies and a waterproof bike cover. The humidity has some unexpected benefits, like cleaner air and trees and greenery.
Not everyone shares my enthusiasm. More than one colleague has been huddled around the office air conditioner complaining about what the humidity is doing to their hair.

Still, once the rain clears, there are few better places to spend an afternoon than the park or a café with outdoor seating. We've always enjoyed these little excursions, but in previous summers they usually required military-style planning to avoid the hottest part of the day. This year we've been able to head out much more spontaneously, without worrying about melting before we reach our destination.
To be honest, though, I've long been an advocate for spending summer in China, even during the hotter years.

Yes, Beijing can become incredibly warm, but the infrastructure is well equipped to deal with it. Air conditioning is commonplace in homes, offices, shops and on public transport, making it surprisingly easy to escape the heat.

Then there's the food. One of my favorite things about summer in China is the seemingly endless selection of cold drinks, desserts and seasonal treats. I've happily sampled everything from tofu lattes and green tea ice cream to more varieties of milk tea than I could count. Half the fun is discovering something new each summer.
And then there are the more traditional ways of cooling down. After living here for so long, spotting someone on the roadside selling refreshing bowl of
southern Chinese style tangshui (a sweet soup) has become one of those unmistakable signs that summer has truly arrived.
Speak to someone with even a basic
understanding of traditional Chinese medicine, however, and they'll probably offer a completely different solution: drink something hot.
As an Englishman, I've never quite
As an Englishman, I've never quite
managed to wrap my head around the
logic of sipping a steaming cup of tea
when it's already 35 degrees outside
managed to wrap my head around the logic of sipping a steaming cup of tea when it's already 35 degrees outside. But then again, who am I to argue with thousands of years of accumulated wisdom?
That's perhaps the biggest lesson I've
learned. People here have generations of experience adapting to hot summers, and that knowledge is reflected everywhere - from architecture and public spaces to food, drinks and everyday habits.
In fact, China's expertise in keeping
cool is now reaching far beyond its borders. Chinese-made air conditioners and other cooling products are becoming popular across Europe, as more households look for relief from hotter summers.
Perhaps my mom's decision to spend

part of her summer in Beijing is simply another example of that trend. Between the excellent infrastructure, endless food options, leafy parks and countless places to cool off, there's always a way to make the most of the season.
And if my mom decides she'd rather
spend future summers in Beijing than sweating through another British heat wave, I don't think she'll be the only foreign traveler thinking along those lines. CBy Michael Jones

hina demands that its residents are flexible and adaptive. In China one must expect the unexpected and be prepared for daily surprises. Indeed, as an outsider, life in China can seem plagued with inconsistencies, and if I could only use one word to describe my life in China, I would choose the word "contrast." This contrast can be seen in all areas of life in China. For example, I have worked for many decisive and cutthroat business leaders, who prioritize harmony within their business practices. I have heard thumping music stirring passion within many parks and tranquil natural valleys. I have seen countless displays of abundant wealth, combined with acts of humility and the respect for simplicity. Welcome to living in the land of yin and yang.

Yin and yang are concepts in Chinese philosophy used to describe how apparently opposite forces are interconnected and interdependent. Rather than being seen as absolute opposites, yin and yang are understood as complementary qualities that exist in balance and can transform into one another. One of the most obvious areas in which China brings together seeming opposites, is in the convergence of the ancient and the modern. China is simultaneously one of the cradles of humanity and yet sits at the cutting edge of modern technology. If you donate money for incense in a historic temple you are far more likely to use your smartwatch than use cash. If you attend a business lecture from a leading entrepreneur, do not be surprised if they connect their business tactics directly to millennia old philosophies. Indeed, while others might see a battle between the old and
China is simultaneously one of the cradles
of humanity and yet sits at the cutting
edge of modern technology
the new, many Chinese people would see China's modern success as a direct result of, and inseparable from, its history.

Yin and yang can be seen in almost every area of Chinese life. For example, Chinese society is in many ways defined by its collective approach to decisions and organization. However, it is also true that one cannot escape the individualistic ambition of Chinese citizens in business, education and the workplace. Whereas many nations debate the relative importance of the individual and the collective, China sees the two as being inherently linked. Likewise, China is a land in which human interactions can feel simultaneously formal and highly structured, while being warm and hospitable. If you visit China, you are highly likely to be invited out for a lavish dinner, at the host's expense, where you will be treated with the utmost generosity. However, the dinner will also have a clear seating plan centred around hierarchy, and the generosity of the hosts will be packaged in a formal respect. Another area of seeming contradiction in China is the variation between vibrant energy and serene calm. In China tranquil tea shops and gardens, where the only sound to be heard is trickling water, sit off busy streets that bustle with mayhem. In China people can sit in silence in a meeting or restaurant, yet burst with noise in a theater or a shop.

At its heart, the philosophy of yin and yang is not about conflict, but about balance, interdependence and change. Often symbolized by the famous blackand-white taijitu, yin and yang represent opposite forces that are not enemies, but partners: dark and light, soft and hard, passive and active, feminine and masculine, rest and motion. Crucially, neither side is presented as wholly good or bad, nor can either exist meaningfully without the other.

In terms of the taijitu the yin is the dark swirl, and the yang is the light one. Yang is harder, stronger, brighter, and faster. Yang is the male, but it has a black feminine dot within it. Meanwhile, yin is the darker swirl, the female. Yin is softer, gentler, darker, and slower, however, there is a white masculine dot within its core. Water flowing calmly in a river is yin, but when it cascades over the rapturous waterfall, that same water is now yang. The states of matter, and people, and life itself are not fixed as yin or yang, one can turn into the other.

The mistake that foreigners often make when they encounter the curious opposites of Chinese life, is that they see conflict and contradiction, where Chinese people simply see balance. China believes that the yin needs the yang, and the yang needs the yin. Therefore, where a foreigner may see competing concepts as being incompatible, Chinese people may see those contrasting elements as owing their very existence and survival to their partnership. By Mina Yan

It's so hot right now, like, everywhere in China! As temperatures soar this summer, an ancient recipe has become the undisputed drink of the season. No, it's not iced coffee or iced tea. It's something many people would never think to try until they've spent some time in China. From the hot, humid streets of Hainan Province to the sweltering tea shops of Beijing and Shanghai, mung bean drinks are the must-have refreshment.

The story of mung bean soup as a summer staple stretches back more than a millennium. Historical records document street vendors selling it during the Tang and Song dynasties (618-1279) on scorching summer days.

So why do Chinese people suddenly start drinking bean soup like it's juice? Its popularity is rooted in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). Mung beans are classified as "cold" in nature, making them the perfect antidote to summer's oppressive heat. In TCM, they're also believed to eliminate toxins, promote urination and relieve heat-related ailments. They're also rich in protein, vitamin C and dietary fiber, aid digestion and stimulate the appetite, which is often suppressed during sweltering weather.

unexpected letdown/hidden pitfall
As temperatures rise, portable fans
have once again become hot sellers. But with so many nearly identical products on the market, consumers can easily cailei by unknowingly buying a poorquality one.
Literally meaning "to step on a land

mine," cailei first gained popularity about a decade ago among investors who bought troubled financial products or fell victim to investment scams. When I was a little kid, my grandma would cook giant batches of mung bean soup every summer. And while Chinese people don't like cold drinks, even the old-timers make an exception for this one. A nice glass of cold mung bean soup is both tasty and packed with medicinal benefits. So when I was little, if I wanted something cold at Grandma's, this was my only choice.

The flavor of well-made mung bean soup is deceptively complex. It's earthy and nutty on the first sip, with an almost grassy sweetness that lingers gently on the palate. The beans are slow-cooked to perfection. Served ice-cold, it's remarkably refreshing: clean, cooling and deeply satisfying, with the added bonus of knowing you're not indulging in a sugary treat but helping your body cope with the summer heat. It's a win-win.

This summer, major milk tea chains have embraced the humble mung bean with creative flair. Even KFC has joined the trend with its Refreshing Mung Bean Drink, featuring soft-cooked mung beans with a hint of mint. If these beverage giants have jumped on board, it's proof this favorite has truly gone mainstream.
But mung bean soup has also sparked

The term has since expanded into everyday language to describe any unpleasant surprise or hidden pitfall that only becomes apparent after making a choice. Examples include buying a product that looks nothing like its online listing, visiting an influencerrecommended restaurant only to find the food disappointing, or traveling for hours to a social media-famous scenic spot that turns out to be no better than one of China's liveliest culinary debates over what color the broth should be.

In the North, where the beans are boiled until they break down and release their starch, the broth takes on a murky reddish-brown or deep olive hue. That's the sign of a properly cooked mung bean soup. Southerners, however, insist it should remain bright translucent green or pale yellowish-green, achieved by briefly boiling the beans with a pinch of salt or a drop of vinegar to preserve the color. Some even steam the beans separately before adding them to clear water.

Social media regularly erupts with passionate arguments, with northerners mocking the southern version as undercooked and southerners dismissing the northern style as muddy bean porridge pretending to be a drink. Despite this enduring culinary divide, one thing is certain: no matter the color, cold mung bean soup is the undisputed champion of Chinese summers.

Today, cailei is commonly used to describe everything from watching disappointing movies to making awkward social remarks that touch on sensitive topics - poor choices that only reveal themselves when it's too late. Its opposite, bilei ("avoid land mines"), is widely used in reviews and recommendations to steer others away from unknowingly crossing into a minefield of errors.
